en: May the lotus-foot of Gaurī, made resonant by the bees swarming from the mass of the immortal goddess’s tresses, dispel all evil. || 1 ||

May the lotus-like feet of Gaurī—which have been made resonant by bees that have settled upon the masses of hair (the tresses) of immortal goddesses out of greed for their fragrance—dispel and destroy all evil and sin. This is a compound formed either according to the *mayūra-vyaṃsaka* rule (where the feet are the lotuses) or as a comparative compound (*upamita-samāsa*) meaning "feet like lotuses.
I praise the ancient husband and wife, the parents of the universe, who have become each other’s fruit through the excellence of their mutual ascetic penance. (2)

We praise the ancient husband and wife, Pārvatī and Parameśvara—the parents and benefactors of the entire universe—who have become the very fruit of each other’s ascetic perfections; that is to say, Parameśvara has become the fruit of the perfection of Pārvatī’s penance, and Pārvatī has become the fruit of the perfection of Parameśvara’s penance. Furthermore, since humility is implied by praise, this constitutes an auspicious invocation in the form of a salutation.
For the sake of enabling beginners to master the ornaments, a charming compendium of their definitions and illustrations is here composed. (3)

Among the ornaments, specifically regarding the figurative ornaments (*arthālaṅkāra*) such as simile (*upamā*) and the rest, this *Lalita*—which is easy to grasp—is composed as a compendium of the definitions and illustrations of those ornaments for the sake of achieving proficiency and mastery among beginners who, despite possessing the capacity for comprehension and retention, remain untrained in the subject of poetic figures. Here, the purpose is stated in the first half [of the verse], and the subject matter to be expounded is proposed in the second half.

A unique property is the definition (*lakṣaṇa*), and that which is to be defined is the illustration (*udāharaṇa*). Thus, the author of the work promises that for the sake of the instruction of beginners, the poetic figures of sense (*arthālaṅkāra*)—beginning with Simile (*upamā*)—will be concisely examined by means of both definitions and illustrations.
Simile (*upamā*) occurs where the beauty of similarity shines forth between two things:
"O Kṛṣṇa, like a female swan, your fame plunges into the celestial Gaṅgā. (4)

In whatever poetry (*kāvyam*) there is the splendor (*lakṣmī*), that is, the excellence (*sampat*) of similarity—meaning a similarity that delights the hearts of connoisseurs—between two things well-known as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), which shines forth, appearing with manifest clarity (without relying on the boundaries of suggestion), that splendor of similarity thus appearing is the definition of *upamā* (simile). "O Kṛṣṇa, your fame plunges into the celestial Gaṅgā like a female swan" is an example.
Here, the splendor of similarity between the fame and the female swan shines forth clearly; thus, it is the figure of speech *upamā*.

An analogy (*upamā*) consists of four components: the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), the object of comparison (*upameya*), the common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*), and the word expressing the analogy (*upamāvācaka*). Among these, the *upamāna*—such as the moon—is that which is renowned for possessing superior qualities. The *upameya*—such as the face—is the subject currently being described and possesses fewer qualities. The *sādhāraṇadharma* is a shared attribute, such as the quality of being delightful. Words such as *iva* are the expressers of similarity. And similarity (*sādṛśya*) is the state of possessing many attributes belonging to one thing while being distinct from it.

In brief, simile (*upamā*) is of two kinds: complete (*pūrṇā*) and elliptical (*luptā*). Where there is the employment of all four components of the simile, it is a complete simile (*pūrṇopamā*), as in the previously cited example beginning with "like a female swan" (*haṃsīva*). Here, the female swan is the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), fame is the object of comparison (*upameya*), bathing in the celestial Gaṅgā is the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*), and the word "like" (*iva*) is the indicator of the simile (*upamāvācaka*). Because all four are employed, it is a complete simile. Another example of the complete simile is:
"The wise man, grasping merits and faults, is like the Lord [Śiva] grasping the moon and poison."
First he praises with his head, then he holds the other by the throat.

In this instance, the wise [poet] has taken the person being compared (*upameya*) as the subject, the Lord (*īśvara*) as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), and the word *iva* as the indicator (*vācaka*). Although there is no single common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*) shared by both the standard and the subject of comparison, nevertheless, because the moon and the poison residing in the standard of comparison and the virtues and defects residing in the subject of comparison are determined to be non-different through the relation of reflection and reflected image (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*), and because the act of grasping and the knowledge [of it] are determined to be non-different through their inclusion within the single word *gṛhṇan*, the status of being a common property is postulated. Therefore, this is indeed a complete simile (*pūrṇopamā*).

In reality, even though the attributes of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) are distinct, their separate mention when they are determined to be non-different due to mutual similarity constitutes the relation of "original and reflection" (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*).
This pertains to the elided simile (*luptopamā*) and its various subdivisions,
concerning the attributes of the subject of description and the standard of comparison, as well as the word expressing the simile.
Due to the non-employment of one, two, or three [elements], the elliptical simile (*luptopamā*) is of eight kinds. (5)

Among the four elements—the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), the object of comparison (*upameya*), the common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*), and the word expressing them (*vācaka*)—the *luptopamā* (elliptical simile) occurs due to the non-employment or omission of one, two, or three of them. It is called "elliptical" (*luptā*) because it is so designated according to its literal meaning (*anvarthasaṃjñā*) based on the omission of constituent parts. The object of description is the *upameya*, while that which is not the object of description is the *upamāna*.

The *luptopamā* (elliptical simile) is divided into eight types, as follows: it is called *vācakaluptā* when there is the elision of the indicator (*vācaka*) alone; *dharmaluptā* when there is the elision of the attribute (*dharma*) alone; *dharmavācakaluptā* when there is the elision of both the attribute and the indicator; *vācakopameyaluptā* when there is the elision of both the indicator and the object of comparison (*upameya*); *upamānaluptā* when there is the elision of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) alone; *vācakopamānaluptā* when there is the elision of both the indicator and the standard of comparison; *dharmopamānaluptā* when there is the elision of both the attribute and the standard of comparison; and *dharmopamānavācakaluptā* when there is the elision of the attribute, the standard of comparison, and the indicator. Examples of elliptical similes are as follows:
"She whose face is like the moon and white as lightning, she who brings camphor-like coolness to my eyes..."
In secret, I beheld that slender woman, who by her loveliness seemed like the very bride of the God of Love.
That meeting with her, and the gain I derived from that passion—
this is all "crow-and-palm" (accidental), occurring without being anticipated.

"She was seen by me in private, a slender girl as fair as lightning"—this is an example of *vācakaluptā* (elliptical simile where the expressive word is omitted). When the intended meaning is "fair like lightning," the compound is formed according to the rule *upamānāni sāmānyavacanaiḥ*; because the expressive word *iva* is elided in this compound, it is called *vācakaluptā*. Here, the slender girl is the object of comparison (*upameya*), lightning is the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), and fairness is the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*).

"Tanvī (the slender one), whose face is like the moon, was seen by me"—this is an example of *dharmaluptā* (omission of the common attribute). "Indutulyāsyā" means "she whose face (*āsya*) is equal (*tulya*) to the moon (*indu*). Here, the moon is the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), the face is the object of comparison (*upameya*), and the word "equal" (*tulya*) is the expressive term (*vācaka*). However, because the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*), such as brilliance (*kānti*) and so forth, is not explicitly mentioned, it is called *dharmaluptā*.

The example of the *dharmavācakaluptā* [simile] is: "karpūrantī tanvī" (the slender girl who acts like camphor). When the intended meaning is "acting like camphor," the suffix *kin*—prescribed by the rule "the suffix *kin* may optionally be added after all nominal stems" (*sarvaprātipadikebhyaḥ kin vā vaktavyaḥ*)—which signifies the sense of "acting" (*ācāra*) in the form of "bestowing joy," is elided along with the word *iva*. Thus, it is a *dharmavācakaluptā*. Here, the two elements—the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), camphor, and the object of comparison (*upameya*), the slender girl—are expressed; however, the quality (*dharma*) consisting of "bestowing joy to the eyes" and its expressive word (*vācaka-śabda*) are not expressed.

"Behaving like the wife of Smara by means of her loveliness" (*kāntyā smaravadhūyantī*) is an example of the *vācakopameyaluptā* (omission of both the expressive word and the object of comparison). Here, when the intended meaning is "acting upon herself as if she were the wife of Smara," the suffix *kyac* is prescribed by the rule *upamānādācāre*. In this case, the self (*ātman*) is the object of comparison (*upameya*), yet it is not expressed; furthermore, the expressive word [for the comparison] is also not expressed. Thus, it is *vācakopameyaluptā*. The wife of Smara is the object of comparison (*upamāna*), and the possession of loveliness is the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*).
In that case, the thought "I shall obtain his semen in that secluded place"—which occurs unexpectedly and by chance—is an example of the *luptopamā* (elliptical simile) known as *kākatālīya*.

*Kākatāla* means "like the crow’s departure and the palm tree’s fall. When the intended meaning is "like the enjoyment of the palm fruit brought about by the crow," the suffix *cha* is prescribed by the rule *samāsācca tadviṣayāt*, which falls under the governing heading *ive pratikṛtau*. Furthermore, by the rule *āyaneyīnīyiyaḥ phaḍhakhañññññṣu*, the substitute *īya* is applied for that suffix. Thus, the derived meaning is: "That object of mine—the slender woman who is like the nectar of the celestial nymphs—whose appearance was unanticipated, is similar to the enjoyment of the palm fruit brought about by the crow."

In this instance, there is the inclusion of three elements: the "attainment of sexual union with a slender woman" (*tanvīsuratalābha*) is the object of comparison (*upameya*), "the state of occurring unexpectedly" (*avitarkitasambhavatva*) is the common attribute (*sādhāraṇo dharmaḥ*), and the suffix *-cha* is the indicator of similarity (*sādṛśyavācaka*). Since the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), namely "the enjoyment of the *kākatāla* fruit," is not explicitly mentioned, it is a case of "elision of the standard of comparison" (*upamānaluptā*). Here, within the compound, the words *kāka* and *tāla* signify, by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the actions inherent in them.

In this regard, my meeting with her, my going there, and her coming there—occurring unexpectedly like the arrival of a crow and the falling of a palm fruit—is expressed by the term *kākatāla*. This is an example of *amānaluptā* (elision of the expressive word). The resulting meaning is that my meeting with her was like the arrival of a crow and the falling of a palm fruit—an occurrence that happened unexpectedly. Here, in the compound *kākatālam*, the expressive word is elided due to the grammatical indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule: "And [the suffix] after a compound referring to such a situation."

The standard of comparison (*upamāna*)—consisting of the crow’s departure and the palm fruit’s fall—is not expressed by a word, even though it is contained within the compound; thus, this is a case of the elision of the expressive standard of comparison (*vācakopamānaluptā*). "My union with him" is the object of comparison (*upameya*), and "accidental occurrence" is the common attribute (*sādhāraṇo dharmaḥ*).

In the illustrative verse, if the reading "iti jānīhi he sakhe" (thus know, O friend) is substituted for "avitarkitasambhavam" (occurring unexpectedly), then even with the elision of the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*), the fifth and sixth [types] become the seventh and eighth examples respectively. The phrase "that I obtain that pleasure is *kākatālīya*" is an example of the elision of both the attribute and the standard of comparison (*dharmopamānaluptā*); whereas the phrase "that I meet her there is *kākatāla*" is an example of the elision of the attribute, the standard of comparison, and the word expressing them (*dharmopamānavācakaluptā*).
[The definition of *Sama* (the Equal): When a single entity possesses the status of both the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object compared (*upameya*), [it is *Sama*].
In such instances as "The moon is like the moon, glorious," there is non-correspondence (ananvaya). ||8||

When both the state of being a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the state of being an object of comparison (*upameya*) are intended for one and the same thing, that is the figure of speech *Ananvaya* (Non-Comparison). It is called *Ananvaya* because the similarity of a thing with itself does not logically follow. The purpose of such a description is to manifest the incomparability [of the subject] by excluding any other similar object. The distinction from the figure of *Upamā* (Simile) is this: in *Upamā*, there is a description of similarity between two distinct things, whereas here it is between one and the very same thing.
In the example, "The moon is like the moon, glorious," the single moon is described as both the standard of comparison and the object of comparison; thus, it is the figure of *Ananvaya*.
The sky is like the sky; the ocean is comparable to the ocean;
the battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa is like [the battle] between Rāma and Rāvaṇa.

In these three types of non-repetition (ananvaya), there is no employment of common attributes (*sādhāraṇadharma*) such as vastness, profundity, or ferocity respectively; however, the distinction is that in the example "The moon is like the glorious moon," there is the employment of all four components [of the simile].
If two things are compared to each other by turns, it is considered Simile of the Compared-to-the-Comparator (*upameyopamā*):
"Dharma is like Artha in its full splendor; Artha is like Dharma in you."

If the status of being the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) is intended to be expressed alternately through distinct sentences for two things—the standard and the object—then it is the figure of speech *upameyopamā* (reciprocal comparison). The essential definition is: where that which was intended as the standard in the first sentence is described as the object in the second, and likewise, that which was the object in the first is described as the standard in the second, that is *upameyopamā*. Its purpose is the exclusion of a third similar object.

"In you, righteousness possesses full splendor like wealth"—this is an example. Here, in the first sentence, righteousness and wealth are respectively the object of comparison (*upameya*) and the standard of comparison (*upamāna*); in the second sentence, their status as the standard of comparison and the object of comparison is described in the same order. Thus, this is the figure of speech *upameyopamā* (reciprocal comparison).
Another example of *upameyopamā* is: "The sky is like the water, and the water is like the sky; the swan is like the moon, and the moon is like the swan."
The stars have the appearance of water-lilies, and the water-lilies have the appearance of stars.

In this case, qualities such as "stainlessness" and "whiteness" are not employed; the distinction is that in the previous example, where it was stated "dharma is like artha," the quality (*dharma*) was indeed employed in the phrase "possessing full splendor" (*pūrṇaśrīḥ*).
First, *pratīpa* (the inverse):
*pratīpa* consists in the conceptualization of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) as the object of comparison (*upameya*).
The lotus is equal to your eye; the moon is like your face.

*Pratīpa* (the "counter-comparison") consists in the conceptualization of something well-known as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), such as the moon, as the object of comparison (*upameya*). It is called *pratīpa* because it is a name that accords with its meaning (*anvarthasaṃjñā*), due to the inversion of the relationship between the well-known standard and object of comparison. "(O slender one,) the lotus is like your eyes" is one example; "the moon is like your face" is another example.

In this regard, in the first instance, the lotus—which is a well-known object of comparison—and in the second, the moon, are both conceived as the objects of comparison (*upameya*); thus the definition is fulfilled. When the object of comparison is conceived as the object of comparison, the status of the original object of comparison as the subject of comparison (*upamāna*) is established. By this, the superiority of the original object of comparison over the [new] object of comparison is illuminated; that indeed is the purpose of *pratīpa*. *Pratīpa* is of five kinds. Among these, this is the first type of *pratīpa*. Another example of the first type of *pratīpa* is: "That blue lotus, which possesses a luster equal to your eyes, has sunk into the water."
O beloved, the moon that mimics the radiance of your face is obscured by clouds;
even those royal swans that followed your departure have gone away.
Fate does not permit me even the mere diversion of your likeness.

Here, *pratīpa* (the inverse) arises from the conceptualization of well-known standards of comparison—such as the blue lotus, the moon, and the royal swan—as the objects of comparison (*upameya*). Its distinction from the previous type lies in the fact that common attributes such as "loveliness" are explicitly mentioned here.
The second type of *pratīpa* consists in the disregard for the subject under description (*varṇya*) due to the availability of another object for comparison.
Enough with your pride; the moon is like your face in its radiance.

The second type of *pratīpa* (the inverse) is that wherein there is disregard for, or the disparagement of, the subject (*varṇya*)—such as the face—which is the actual object of description (*upameya*), by means of the attainment or acquisition of another object of comparison (*upamāna*) that is not itself being described. Although the conceptualization of the object of comparison as the object of description is common to both [types], the specific distinction here is the disregard for the subject. An example is: "O Face! Enough with your pride; let there be no pride, for even the moon, by virtue of its quality of luster, is like you."

Here, because the described face attains the status of the object of comparison (upameya) by means of the non-described moon, there is a fulfillment of the definition through the description of disregard in the form of the thought, "Let there be no pride.
This is another example of the second type of *pratīpa* (the inverse).
"O blessed lady, why do you carry this unbearable pride with your pair of eyes?"
Surely there are such blue lotuses in the lakes in every direction.

Here, by conceiving the blue lotuses as the objects of comparison (*upameya*), disregard is shown toward the pair of eyes—the subject of description—in order that they may not harbor pride; however, because the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) is not explicitly mentioned, this differs from the previous example.
The third type of *pratīpa* consists of disregard for another [subject] through the attainment of the status of being the object of comparison for the subject under description.
O Death, what pride of cruelty do you possess? For there are indeed women equal to you. ||12||

The third type of *pratīpa* (the inverse) is likewise [defined] as the disregard for another, unpraiseworthy object—a well-known standard of comparison—by means of obtaining that which is being praised, namely the subject of description (*upameya*). The meaning is that this variety of *pratīpa* consists in showing disregard for the unpraiseworthy subject by displaying the praiseworthy subject of description, because the former cannot tolerate the latter's superior qualities. For example: "O Death! Enough with your pride in cruelty; let there be no pride in you, for there are women equal to you in ferocity."

Here, the subject of description (*upameya*) is cruel women; because of the description of their disregard for death—the unmentioned subject of comparison (*upamāna*)—which is well-known in its cruelty due to the attainment of those women, the definition [of *pratīpa*] is fully applicable. This is indeed a *pratīpa* based on the very opposite of the second type of *pratīpa*. This point must be considered here: the name *pratīpa* has been given as a literal designation (*anvartha*), because it is the reverse of the well-established relationship between the object of comparison and the standard of comparison.

If that were the case, how could one conceive of it as a variety of *pratīpa* (the inverse) in instances where such a counter-attraction (*prātilomya*) does not exist? In fact, its enumeration as a variety of *pratīpa* is not appropriate. It appears more fitting to designate it as "disregarding simile" (*anādaropamā*), having conceived it as a sub-variety of simile. Furthermore, the definition that it is called *pratīpa* because it is the reverse of the previously mentioned *pratīpa* is not correct.
Another example of the third type of *pratīpa* is:
"O Hālāhala poison! Do not be arrogant, thinking 'I alone am the teacher of all things most cruel'."
Surely there exist many more such words of the wicked in this world as those spoken by you.

In this matter of cruelty, because the object of comparison—consisting of the speech of the wicked—is obtained as being equal to *hālāhala* (poison), there is a disregard for the unpraised *hālāhala* itself; this is the third type of *pratīpa*.
The fourth type of *pratīpa* is the statement that the comparison of another [object] with the subject of description is not accomplished.
"O lovely-eyed one, it is a false accusation that the lotus merely resembles your face. (13)

The fourth type of *pratīpa* (the inverse), which possesses even greater excellence than the previous types, consists in the statement that the similarity (*sādṛśya*)—that is, the comparison—is not established between the described subject (*varṇya*), such as the face, and another, undescribed object (*avarṇya*), such as the moon (conceived as the *upameya*). An example is: "O lovely-eyed one, the lotus resembles your face; it possesses a beauty equal to your face"—this report is a futile slander, a false rumor among the people. (The word *kila* indicates hearsay. This is the illustration.

Here, the non-establishment of similarity between the lotus—the well-known standard of comparison (*upamāna*)—and the heroine’s face—the object of comparison (*upameya*)—is expressed by the phrase "vain reproach" (*mudhāpavāda*); thus, the definition [of *pratīpa*] is fully applicable. Listen to another example of the fourth type of *pratīpa*: "O lotus-eyed one, this reproach on earth..."
The moon is compared by the vulgar to your face.

In this case, the similarity between the face and the moon is stated only by common folk (*pāmaras*); and since that [statement] is censurable, it is thereby revealed that the similarity itself is unestablished.
The fifth type of *pratīpa* (the inverse) is considered to be even the uselessness of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*).
If the face of the slender maiden has been seen, what need is there for a lotus or the moon?

The fifth type of *pratīpa* (the inverse) consists in stating the pointlessness (*kaimarthya*)—that is, the uselessness—of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), such as the moon, [on the grounds that] a subject of comparison (*upameya*) possessing equal qualities has been found. For example: "If the face of the slender maiden has been seen, what is the use of the lotus or the moon? The meaning is that there is no purpose whatsoever [for them]. Here, because a face possessing equal qualities—the object of comparison—is obtained, the lack of utility for the well-known standards of comparison, the lotus and the moon, is demonstrated; thus the definition is consistent.
[Etymologically: "What is the purpose (*artha*) of this? is *kimartha*; the state of being so is *kaimarthya*.
Another example of the fifth type of *pratīpa* (the contrary):
"Whenever [the poet] conceives in his mind that these two [the moon and the sun] exist in vain compared to his [the king's] power and his fame,
then Fate, under the pretext of a halo around the sun, causes even the moon to form a ring."

In this case, since the presence of Nala’s prowess and fame is established, the sun and moon are rendered useless; thus, because of the statement regarding the futility of the two well-known standards of comparison, the sun and moon, this is *pratīpa* (the inverse).

That which consists of the coloring of the subject (*viṣaya*) by means of its identity with or similarity to the object (*viṣayin*) is *rūpaka* (metaphor); it is of three kinds through expressions of superiority, inferiority, or neither. (15)

The *viṣayin* (the possessor of the attribute) is the object of comparison, such as a lotus; the *viṣaya* (the subject of comparison) is that which is being compared, such as a face. *Rūpaka* (metaphor) is the coloring of the *viṣaya* by means of the form of the *viṣayin*, through either non-difference (*abheda*) or identity of form (*tādūpya*), whereby it becomes the object of a cognition colored by itself. This coloring of the *viṣaya*—which is expressed by its own word—in the form of the *viṣayin*, results in some cases in the non-difference from the well-known *viṣayin*, and in other cases, while difference remains perceived, it results merely in the superimposition of the attributes belonging to that [viṣayin].

Furthermore, *rūpaka* (metaphor) is of two kinds: *abhedarūpaka* (metaphor of identity) and *tādrūpyarūpaka* (metaphor of resemblance). Each of these two types is again threefold, depending on whether the object (*viṣaya*) is described as being superior to, inferior to, or neither superior nor inferior to the subject (*viṣayin*). Thus, *rūpaka* is sixfold: *anubhayābhedarūpaka*, *nyūnābhedarūpaka*, *adhikābhedarūpaka*, *anubhayatādrūpyarūpaka*, *nyūnatādrūpyarūpaka*, and *adhikatādrūpyarūpaka*.

These six have been explained here according to the order of their examples, rather than the order indicated by the root verses. The examples are presented in this very sequence. Here is an example of the non-dual metaphor (*abhedarūpaka*) that is neither [of the two previous types]:
"For this is indeed Śiva himself, by whom the cities were burnt in an instant."

"This king standing before me is Śiva, Dhūrjaṭi himself, by whom the enemy cities were burnt to ashes in an instant"—this is an example of the *anubhayābheda-rūpaka* (metaphor of non-difference between neither). Here, due to the similarity of being a burner of cities (*puradāhakatva*), the non-difference "this is indeed Śambhu himself" is perceived. Since neither the deficiency nor the excess of the subject (*viṣaya*) is mentioned, the definition [of the metaphor] is fully applicable. Another example of this very same [type] is:
"On this sandy bank of the Sarayū, brightened by the moonlight..."
A long debate took place between two young Siddhas:
one says Kaiṭabha was slain first, the other says Kaṃsa.
"Therefore, tell us the truth, O Blessed One! Which of them was killed first?"

Here, by the phrase "you yourself" (*sa tvam*), the non-difference between the slayer of Kaṃsa and Kaiṭabha and the one bearing the Garuḍa-banner (Viṣṇu) is established regarding the subject of description. Furthermore, through the pretext of questioning the chronological order of the slaying of Kaṃsa and Kaiṭabha, that very non-difference is reinforced; it is not, however, intended to establish either deficiency or excess. Thus, this is a *non-difference metaphor* (*abhedarūpaka*) of the "neither-nor" type (*anubhaya*). An example of a *non-difference metaphor* of the "deficient" (*nyūna*) type is as follows:
"This [face] remains, lacking Śambhu’s third eye. (16)

"This King standing before us is Śambhu, yet he remains without the third eye"—this is an example of *nyūnābhedarūpaka* (metaphor of identity with deficiency). Here, although the identity between the subject of description, the king, and Śiva is established, a deficiency is stated in the form of his lack of a third eye; thus, the definition is fully applicable.
Another example of this very same [figure] is:
"The Creator created a twofold delusion regarding beautiful women and gold."
Unattached even to those [objects] among them, he is the manifest splendor (Bharga) in human form.

In this instance, since the non-difference between the dispassionate one and Śiva is established by the statement "the dispassionate one is directly Bharga," and because the phrase "having a human form" establishes the subject's lack of a divine form, this is a *nyūnābheda-rūpaka* (metaphorical identification of inferiority).
An example of *adhikābheda-rūpaka* (metaphorical identification of superiority) is:
"Today Śambhu protects the universe, having assumed an impartial vision."

In this context, the word "this" (*ayam*) is to be supplied from the preceding example. "This Śambhu, today, by adopting an equal gaze—that is, an equal number of eyes (and by seeing all things in one form)—protects the universe. This is an example of the *adhikābhedarūpaka* (superlative identity metaphor). Here, having established the non-difference [of the king] with Śambhu through the statement "this king is indeed Śambhu," the superiority of the subject is demonstrated by showing that whereas he previously had an unequal gaze, he now possesses an equal gaze; thus, the definition is fully applicable. "Superiority" (*ādhikya*) means excellence.
Another example of this very same [figure] follows:
Why does this ocean tremble at your arrival?
Do you fear him because you were the one who built the bridge?
For even on another island, he is not now subject to your will.
O bull among kings! Fortune attends you who serve her.

In this verse, by the phrase "you, the maker of the bridge and the churning-stick," the non-difference between the King and Nārāyaṇa is established. Since all other islands have been brought under his control, there is no longer anything left to conquer; and since he has already attained the Goddess of Fortune (Lakṣmī), there is no further occasion for churning. Thus, because his excellence is manifested in comparison to his former state, this is an *adhika-abheda-rūpaka* (hyperbolic metaphor of identity).
An example of *anubhayatādrūpya-rūpaka* (metaphor of identity where neither [the subject nor the object] is explicitly stated) is:
"Now that the joy of the eyes has been obtained through her moon-like face, what need is there for the [celestial] moon? (17)

The face alone of this slender lady is the moon; since the joy of the eyes has been obtained by that "moon-face," what is the use of the [actual] moon? It means there is no purpose whatsoever, because the function of the moon—namely, the delighting of the eyes—is accomplished by the face alone. Here, although a distinction between the face and the moon is perceived, the superimposition of "moon-ness" upon the face in the phrase "by the moon-face" results merely in the superimposition of its attribute, namely, the quality of causing delight to the eyes. Furthermore, because neither deficiency nor excess is mentioned, it is also a case of non-dual (anubhayatāpa) metaphor.
Here is another example of this very same type:

Does your moon-like face not destroy the luster of the lotus, does it not bestow joy upon the eyes, does it not increase the passion of the flower-bannered god, and does it not, by its mere appearance, perform all that? Indeed, it is true that another cool-rayed moon has arisen!
If pride were to arise from nectar here, it already exists indeed in her bimba-fruit-like lower lip.

Here, although the difference between the object (*viṣaya*) and the object of comparison (*viṣayin*), namely the face and the moon, is perceived, the superimposition of "moon-ness" upon the face in the phrase *vaktrendau* culminates merely in its performing the functions of the moon; because neither excellence nor inferiority is expressed, this is a case of "metaphor of neither identity nor difference" (*anubhayatādrūpya-rūpaka*).
An example of the "metaphor of inferiority" (*nyūnatādrūpya-rūpaka*) is:
"This virtuous woman is another Lakṣmī, arisen from the ocean of nectar."

This virtuous, devoted wife, born from the ocean of nectar, is another Lakṣmī who has not arisen from the Ocean of Milk. Here, by the expression "another Lakṣmī," a distinction from the well-known Lakṣmī is understood regarding this woman. Thus, the attribution of "Lakṣmī-hood" to the virtuous woman culminates in the attribution of a single attribute. Furthermore, by the statement of her inferiority—namely, that she was "not born from the ocean of nectar"—this constitutes a *nyūnatādṛpya-rūpaka* (metaphor of inferiority).
Another example of this very same [type] is:
"Brahmā is not four-faced; Hari is another, having but two arms."
The blessed Śambhu Bādarāyaṇa has eyes that do not blink.

Here, because Brahmā and the others perceive a difference [from Bādarāyaṇa], there is the metaphor of "coloring" (tādrūpyarañjana). Since deficiency is also expressed by the phrase "not possessing the four Vedas" and so forth, this is the metaphor of "deficiency as identity" (nyūnatādrūpyarūpaka).
An example of the metaphor of "superiority as identity" (adhikatādrūpyarūpaka) is:
"This moon of a face surpasses the spotted moon. (18)

This face standing before me is indeed the moon; this "moon-face" surpasses—that is, excels—the "stained moon," the well-known moon, because it is free from a stain (*kalaṅka*). (Here too, the superimposition of the nature of the moon upon the face results in the superimposition of its attributes alone, since the distinction [between the two] is still perceived; and because the excellence of the moon-face is established through its being devoid of a stain, this is an *adhikatādrūpyarūpaka* [a metaphor of superior identity].
Another example of this very same [type] is:
"O dull-witted one! Do you think that by these withered breaths [of life], the mind of Bhīma’s daughter might sink into me?"
Indeed, the wise god of love declared that my Veda has that [moon] as its meaning, for it is intent upon the moon-like face of Nala.

In this instance, regarding Damayantī’s reproach of the moon, the well-known moon is not the intended object (*tātparyaviṣaya*) of the Vedic scripture which speaks of the entry of the mind at the time of the departure of life; rather, it is the moon that is Nala’s face. Since this establishes the superiority (*utkarṣa*) of Nala’s facial moon over the well-known moon, it is a *rūpaka* (metaphor) consisting of "superiority in identity" (*adhikatādrūpyarūpaka*). As for the ornament of *pariṇāma*: "Pariṇāma occurs when the subject (*viṣayin*), for the sake of an action, assumes the nature of the object (*viṣaya*)."
The intoxicating-eyed woman gazes with her lotus-like eye, clear and serene.

When the object of comparison (*viṣayin*), as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), is for the sake of an action—that is, if it is useful for the matter at hand (*prakṛtakārya*)—it is the figure of speech *pariṇāma*. Here too, as in *rūpaka*, there is superimposition (*āropa*). However, the distinction is that the superimposed object (*āropyamāṇa*), the *viṣayin*, becomes useful for the purpose by taking on the form of the subject (*viṣaya*); in *rūpaka*, this is not the case. Thus is the difference between the two. Superimposition (*āropa*) is the apprehension of non-difference between the subject and the object of comparison when they are indicated by their own respective words.

"Madirekṣaṇā" means one with beautiful eyes; "tanvī" [is used here]. She gazes—that is, she sees—with an eye that is like a lotus, being clear and stainless. This is the illustration. Here, the nature of a lotus is superimposed upon the eye (the organ of sight). Since its connection with the primary action of gazing would not be possible in its own form, it is called *pariṇāma* (transformation/metaphorical transformation) because it becomes useful for the action only through its transformation into the nature of the object of comparison (the eye). Thus, the name is significant to its meaning. Having crossed the celestial river, which is the garland upon the head of the Lord of Beings (Śiva), by means of himself as the third [person], he (Rāma) provided the ferryman with a fare consisting of his friendship with the son of Sumitrā (Lakṣmaṇa).

Then, followed with difficulty for a moment by Śabara maidens whose breasts were as large as a fathom and whose eyes were upturned in curiosity, he set out for Citrakūṭa, the mountain that never wavers.

Here, the state of being a brother (*bhrātṛtva*) is superimposed upon the friendship with the son of Sumitrā (*saumitrimaitrī*). And that superimposed brotherhood, by assuming the form of the friendship with the son of Sumitrā—which is the locus of the superimposition—becomes useful for the purpose of Guha’s assistance, but not in its own right, because Guha has no need for wages; thus, this is the figure of speech *pariṇāma* (transformation).
First, regarding *ullekha* (multiple description): it is intended as the multiple description of a single object by many people in various ways.
He was regarded as the god of love by women, as the wish-fulfilling tree by those seeking wealth, and as Death itself by his enemies.

Ullekha (the figure of speech "Depiction") is of two kinds: that which consists in the depiction of a single object possessing various attributes by many perceivers in multiple ways, and that which consists in the depiction of a single object by a single perceiver in multiple ways. Herein, the definition and illustration of the first type are set forth in this verse. It is called Ullekha—a name significant to its meaning—an ornament consisting in the subject being apprehended or depicted in many ways, through many different modes, by many diverse perceivers, as characterized by various attributes.

This king, endowed with beauty, generosity, and prowess, was perceived by women as Kāma (Love); (he was taken by them to be Madana). He was perceived by supplicants as the *svadru* tree, the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*); (it was inferred that he was indeed the wish-fulfilling tree). He was perceived by enemies as Kāla, the Ender (*antaka*); (he was seen as the Ender). Such is the illustration.

Here, the application of the definition is as follows: a single king, characterized by numerous attributes such as beauty and so forth, is depicted in many ways—as Cupid, Indra, and Yama—by many supplicants and enemies respectively. In *ullekha* (multiple description), as in *rūpaka* (metaphor), there is superimposition (*āropa*) in many instances; however, the distinction is that here, due to the difference in perceivers or the difference in objects, there is a superimposition of many subjects upon a single object, whereas in *rūpaka*, this is not the case.
Another example of this *ullekha* is: "He is the 'Protector of Elephants' by the elderly women, and the 'Beloved of Śrī' by the young maidens."
And Śauri, as he actually was, was gazed upon by the child with curiosity.

In that context, as Kṛṣṇa enters Dvārakā, he is depicted in many ways by numerous people, such as the elders, on account of his being the savior of the elephant and so forth. The distinction here is that while there was a presence of superimposition (*āropa*) in the previous example, making it a mixture with metaphor (*rūpaka*), that is not the case here.
The second type of *ullekha* occurs when a single subject is depicted in many ways due to a difference in perspectives (*viṣayabheda*).
"In speech this Arjuna is my teacher; in fame, Bhīṣma; but in the wielding of the bow, this one [Arjuna]. (21)

The word "of one" (*ekasya*) is supplied from the preceding verse. Even when a single object—though qualified by many attributes—is apprehended in many ways, that is, represented in various modes according to the distinctions of its aspects by a single perceiver, this constitutes the figure of speech *ullekha* (multiple description).

This king standing before us is Bṛhaspati, the great preceptor, in the matter of speech; Arjuna Pārtha, the white one, in the matter of fame; and Bhīṣma, the son of Gaṅgā, the terrifying one, in the matter of the bow. Here, the single king alone is depicted in many ways—specifically in two modes—by a single perceiver through the distinction of objects such as speech and so forth; thus the definition is fulfilled.
Another example of the second type of *ullekha* (multiple description) is:
"Not thin at the breasts, thin at the waist, broad at the eyes, and expansive at the hips..."
May the dawn-red appear upon the lower lip, and may the fortune of the compassionate face of the Lord of Kapila manifest within the heart.

Here, the form of Pārvatī, determined as the share of Kapālin (Śiva), is made the object of a single perceiver through many modes—such as "not being thin" and so forth—due to the difference in objects such as her breasts and other parts; this is the second type of *ullekha* (multiple description).
There may also be three varieties of its ornaments: those based on memory (*smṛti*), error (*bhrānti*), and doubt (*sandeha*).

When [an object] is represented through memory, error, or doubt based on similarity, there arise three figures of speech marked by the terms "memory," "error," and "doubt"; that is to say, there are three figures of speech—respectively *smṛtimān*, *bhrāntimān*, and *sandeha*. Their definitions are, respectively, the state of being memory (*smṛtitva*), the state of being error (*bhrāntitva*), and the state of being doubt (*sandehatva*). Since these—beginning with memory—are rooted in similarity and possess aesthetic charm (*camatkāritva*), their status as figures of speech is established.

And "being memory" (*smṛtitva*) is a specific universal (*jāti*) evidenced by the experience "I remember. "Error-ness" (*bhramatva*) is the state of being a cognition whose qualifier does not reside in the qualificandum. "Doubt-ness" (*sandehatva*) is the state of being a cognition of the possession of various contradictory properties in a single substratum.

Thus, the established meaning is as follows: when one describes the recollection of one thing upon seeing another due to a similarity recognized by poets, it is the *smṛtimat* (recollection) ornament; when one describes a delusion regarding the object (*viṣaya*)—such as a face—by mistaking it for the correlate (*viṣayin*)—such as a lotus—it is the *bhrāntimat* (delusion) ornament; and when one describes doubt due to the failure to perceive the distinction between two similar things, the object and the correlate, it is the *sandeha* (doubt) ornament.
An example of the *smṛtimat* ornament is: "As I gaze at the lotus, my mind plunges into the face of my beloved. (22)

In the verse, "As I behold the lotus, my mind plunges into the face of my beloved, remembering it," the figure of speech is *smṛtimat* (remembrance), because the description of the recollection of the beloved's face—similar to the lotus—is occasioned by the sight of the lotus.
Another example of this very same [figure] is:
"Before her, she caused even the gods to be filled with wonder..."
Beholding a certain woman emerging from the water like the goddess Śrī, her beautiful hands shimmering with lotuses,
Śauri recalled the churning of the ocean.

In this case, as Kṛṣṇa gazes upon a certain beautiful woman entering the water during a water-sport, the recollection of the churning of the ocean—which shares similar splendor—is described following his memory of that [ocean's] beauty; this is the distinction from the previous example.
An example of the *bhrāntimān* (error) ornament is:
"This intoxicated bee mistakes your face for a lotus."

This intoxicated bee, overcome by passion, perceives—that is, recognizes—your face as a lotus; it forms the cognition that your face is a lotus. Because this describes a cognition characterized by the quality of "being a lotus" with respect to a face which lacks the status of being a lotus, based on the cause of similarity, this is the figure of speech *bhrāntimān* (Error).
Another example of this very same [figure] is: "The bee falls upon the parrot’s beak, mistaking it for a palāśa flower."
He too, mistaking it for a rose-apple fruit, desired to seize that bee.
In this instance, the bee mistakes the parrot’s beak for a *palāśa* flower, while the parrot mistakes the bee for a *jambū* fruit; this description of mutual delusion constitutes the distinction.
An example of the figure of speech *sandeha* (doubt) is as follows:
"Is it a lotus, or is it the moon? For us, however, there is no certainty. (23)

Upon seeing a face or a lotus, one hesitates, thinking, "Is this a lotus, or is it the nectar-rayed moon? Since there is no certainty for us here, the cognition involving both alternatives—being a lotus and being the moon—is rooted in similarity; thus, this is the figure of speech *sandeha* (doubt).
Another example of this very same [figure] is:
"Bending down when grasping for life, yet rising high once they have grasped it."
Are these wicked people the younger ones or the elder ones of the water-wheel?

In this case, the doubt raised by the wicked—whether the water-wheel is the elder sister or the younger—is one whose alternatives (*koṭi*) are purely imaginary; however, in the previous example, the alternatives were well-known. This is the distinction.

*Apahnuti* (concealment) is a negation, and it is an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) preceded by the cognition of non-difference based on similarity. *Apahnuti* is of six kinds: pure concealment (*śuddhāpahnuti*), concealment by means of a reason (*hetvapahnuti*), inverted concealment (*paryastāpahnuti*), concealment through error (*bhrāntāpahnuti*), clever concealment (*chekāpahnuti*), and deceitful concealment (*kaitavāpahnuti*). The definitions and examples of these are shown in order. First, pure concealment (*śuddhāpahnuti*):
The concealment of a quality for the purpose of superimposing another is the removal of purity.
"This is not the moon; what then? It is a lotus in the celestial Ganges. (24)

Pure Apahnuti (simple concealment) is the denial of a quality of the subject (*upameya*) for the purpose of superimposing another, extraneous quality; its fruit is such superimposition. The essential definition is: pure Apahnuti is the negation of a quality of the subject, which has as its result the attribution of a quality belonging to the object of comparison (*upamāna*). An example is: "This visible thing in the sky is not the nectar-rayed moon, but rather a lotus of the celestial Ganges."

In this case, for the purpose of superimposing the state of being a lotus in the celestial Ganges—which resembles it—upon the moon that is the subject of description, the denial of its own [the moon’s] lunar nature is made; thus, this is *śuddhāpahnuti* (pure concealment). Although there is a superimposition here as well, just as in *rūpaka* (metaphor), the distinction is that in *rūpaka* there is no denial of the actual property (*prakṛtadharmāniṣedha*).
Another example of *śuddhāpahnuti* is:
"Some suspected it to be a mark; others considered it the mud of the ocean."
Some declared it to be a spotted deer, while others maintained it was the shadow of the earth;
for that which appears on the moon as dark as a fragment of split sapphire,
we say it is the thick, swallowed-up darkness residing within its belly during the night.

In this instance, while the moon is visible, for the purpose of superimposing the nature of "darkness" upon the dark object, there is a negation not only of its inherent qualities but also of those qualities imagined by others; this is the distinction. Herein lies a further aesthetic charm (*vaicitrya*) consisting in the negation of multiple attributes at once. Since qualities such as being a "mark" (*aṅka*) or being "mud" (*paṅka*) are presented as the views of others, their negation is established by implication (*arthasiddha*).
When that same [negation] is preceded by a logical reason (*yukti*), it is called "Negation based on a Reason" (*hetvapahnuti*).
This fierce roar that has arisen from the ocean is neither dry nor constant. ||25||

That very same [figure], when the negation of the subject matter (*prakṛtadharma*) is performed for the purpose of superimposing something else, preceded by reasoning and provided with a cause, is *hetvapahnuti*. The essential definition is: where there is a negation of the subject matter intended to result in the superimposition of something non-subject (*aprakṛta*), and a reason is also specified therein, that is *hetvapahnuti*.

"This object seen in the sky is not the moon, for it is sharp and exceedingly hot; nor is it the sun, because it is seen at night. It is the Aurva [fire] risen from the ocean"—this is the example. Here, in the negation of being the moon and being the sun, "sharpness" and "being seen at night" are respectively stated as the reasons. And this negation is for the purpose of superimposing the nature of the Aurva fire upon the moon under discussion; such is the synthesis of the definition.
Furthermore, the description of the moon as "sharp" is justified because these are the words of a woman separated from her lover.
Here is another illustration of this very point:
the scar from the wound caused by the friction of thousands of boulders at the base of Mount Mandara shines in the midst of the moon.
To call them "the deer of the shadow" or "the rabbit" is the speech of the most vulgar;
for in no way whatsoever can they possibly be connected with those [reflections].

In this case, there is a logical possibility only for the moon to possess a scar caused by the impact of the Mandara mountain during the churning of the ocean, and not for shadows and the like; thus, the denial (*apahnava*) of those [other possibilities] is revealed through the citation of the speech of a commoner (*pāmara*). Here, by the word "shadow" (*chāyā*), the shadow of the earth is intended.
This is a "transferred denial" (*paryastāpahnuti*); for it is defined as: "Transferred denial is that which serves to superimpose [the subject] upon something else."
This is not the moon; what then? It is the face of my beloved, which is the true moon.

Where there is the concealment of a particular attribute in one object, for the purpose of superimposing that same attribute upon another object intended for description, there occurs *paryastāpahnuti*. Since it is a negation (*apahnuti*) that is "reversed" (*paryasta*)—meaning the negation has a different locus from the superimposition—it is appropriately named *paryastāpahnuti*.

"This one seen before us is not the Sudhāṃśu [the Nectar-rayed One], it is not the moon, but rather the face of my beloved is the Sudhāṃśu"—this is an example. Here, the negation of the status of being the Sudhāṃśu in the moon is for the purpose of superimposing that status of being the Sudhāṃśu upon the face of the beloved, who is the subject of description elsewhere; such is the application of the definition. (Although the negation of "moon-ness" in the moon does not directly serve the purpose of superimposing it upon the face, the statement that it serves that purpose is made because its function in producing the firmness of the superimposition is established by experience.
Another example of this follows.
Hālāhala is not truly poison; rather, O people, Lakṣmī is the poison—yet here, people consider this to be a reversal. 26.
Having drunk from her, Śiva remains awake in happiness; yet Hari, touching her, falls into a deep sleep.

In this instance, the denial of the poisonous nature of the *hālāhala* poison is for the purpose of superimposing it upon *Ramā*. The distinction from the previous example is that a reason (*hetu*) is also stated in the second half of the verse. Thus, it should be understood that *paryastāpahnuti* (inverted concealment) is also twofold: by the non-statement and by the statement of a reason. *Bhrāntāpahnuti* (concealment of error):
*Bhrāntāpahnuti* occurs when an error is prevented following a suspicion regarding something else.
It causes a feverish heat accompanied by trembling—is it a physical fever? No, my friend, it is the God of Love!

When there is a suspicion—that is, when an error (*bhrama*) regarding something else, namely that which is other than the true nature (*prakṛtetara*), exists; and when there is the warding off of that error, or its removal through the proclamation of the truth (*tattvākhyāna*), it is *bhrāntāpahnuti* because of the negation of the object of the error. The essential point is: the negation of the object of an error caused by the statement of the truth. A heroine afflicted by love, keeping the God of Love in mind, says: "He causes trembling and fever."

Because trembling and feverish heat are common to both physical illness and love, a friend of straightforward intellect suspects, “Is this a fever? The heroine, however, dispels her friend’s doubt by first stating the truth—“It is not a fever, but Love”—thereby negating the fever that was the object of her friend’s delusion. Thus, the half-verse beginning with “It causes heat... (*tāpaṃ karoti...*) is an example of *bhrāntāpahnuti* (concealment by means of a mistaken perception). When a delusion arises due to resemblance, it is the figure of speech *bhrāntimad* (delusive); when that [delusion] is subsequently negated, it is *bhrāntāpahnuti*. Here is another example of this [figure]:
This buffalo here, with its tail on both sides, is a sign of the excessive prosperity of the citizens.
"No, no! This is a young elephant; this is its trunk, not its tail."

In this case, there is a misconception of a buffalo in a young elephant, which takes the form of a certainty (*niścaya*). The distinction from the previous example, "Is it a fever?", is that there the misconception takes the form of doubt (*sandeha*). Furthermore, when a villager’s misconception of a buffalo in a young elephant and his misconception of a tail in the trunk are dispelled by a city-dweller through the prior revelation of the truth, this is *bhrāntāpahnuti* (concealment of error).
Chekāpahnuti (Artful Concealment): Chekāpahnuti occurs when there is the denial of a reality due to a suspicion regarding something else.
"Is this my beloved clinging to my feet while speaking? No, it is certainly not; it is an anklet. (28)

*Chekāpahnuti* (clever denial) occurs when, due to the apprehension of another person who has not been specifically addressed—meaning, for the sake of removing that apprehension caused by a suspicion regarding the reality of the matter—there is a concealment or denial of the actual, true, intended meaning. The definition of the term is as follows: *cheka* means clever or skillful; *apahnuti* is denial; thus, *che kāpahnuti* is a denial performed by a clever person. The formal definition is: the negation of a suspected real object through a different interpretation of the sentence.

“*Prajalpan matpade lagnaḥ*... and so forth is an example. A certain heroine, keeping her beloved in mind, says to a trusted female friend: “While prattling about something or other [in order to conciliate me], he has clung to my feet—that is, prostrated at my feet. A certain untrustworthy woman, having heard those words by chance and suspecting the true state of affairs, asks: “What is the lover saying?”

Then the clever heroine, in order to conceal the truth, replies: "It is not my beloved, but rather the anklet. Here, by reinterpreting the sentence—"it is the anklet alone that is making a sound and clinging to the foot"—she negates the suspected real object, the beloved, through her wit; thus the definition is fulfilled.
Another example of this very same [figure] is: "It teaches the *sītkāra* [sound of pleasure], it wounds the lower lip, and it spreads horripilation..."

"Has a lover (*nāgarika*) met [you]? "No, no, friend! It is the winter wind. Having heard these words—"Here it teaches one to shiver"—spoken by someone to her dear friend with the intention of referring to a lover, another woman suspects the literal meaning. To dispel that suspicion regarding her, the speaker describes the sentence as being concerned with the winter wind, thereby effecting a concealment (*apahnava*) of the actual lover. This is *kaitavāpahnuti* (concealment by pretext).
Disguised Denial (*kaitavāpahnuti*) occurs when there is a concealment by means of words such as "pretext" (*vyāja*) once the [hidden] reality has been revealed:
"The arrows of Love depart under the pretext of the glances cast by my beloved. (29)

*Kaitavāpahnuti* (concealment by deceit) occurs when a negation (*nihnuteḥ*)—that is, a denial—is manifested or made clear through words such as "pretext" (*vyāja*), "guile" (*chala*), "deceit" (*kaitava*), and so forth. In this case, the negation of a quality is not performed directly by the particle *nañ*, but rather the negation is understood through words like "deceit" which express its unreality. An example is: "Under the pretext of her glances"—meaning by way of the spreading of the beloved's gaze—the arrows of Love, those specific shafts of the God of Desire, go forth or emerge.
Here, by the word "kaitava" (deceit), the concealment (*apahnava*) is perceived: "These are not the side-glances of a beloved, but rather the arrows of the God of Love.
Here is another example of this:
"In the hollows of the forest, which are empty save for talk of water, [the travelers] are scorched by the heat of the great midday sun expanding its scorching rays."
Under the guise of the flames of a forest fire arising from within their trunks, the trees extend their tongues and beg for water.

In this passage, by means of the pretext of the flames of a forest fire, trees scorched by the summer heat are requesting water; through this deceptive expression (*chalapada*), it is understood that "these are not flames of a forest fire, but rather the tongues of the trees.
Poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) may consist of a thing, a cause, or an effect;
it is said to have its locus either expressed or unexpressed, and furthermore, it is classified as having its basis established or unestablished. (30)

*Saṃbhāvanā* (poetic fancy) is *utprekṣā*. "Utprekṣā" is the mention of the term to be defined (*lakṣya-nirdeśa*), while "saṃbhāvanā" is the definition (*lakṣaṇa*). Saṃbhāvanā is a cognition distinct from both certainty and doubt; some maintain that saṃbhāvanā is a doubt characterized by one alternative being more prominent (*utkaṭaikatarakoṭikaḥ saṃśayaḥ*). The essential meaning (*niṣkarṣa*) is this: *utprekṣā* is the fancying of identity between one thing and another, based on a cause consisting in the connection with the attributes of the former.

Poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) is threefold: poetic fancy as a thing (*vastu*), or rather, poetic fancy as an essential nature (*svarūpa*), poetic fancy as a cause (*hetu*), and poetic fancy as an effect (*phala*). Poetic fancy as a thing is the imagining of a certain thing as being identical with another thing. And "thing-ness" (*vastutva*) consists in being distinct from that which is intended [as the subject] by way of being a cause or an effect. Poetic fancy as a cause is the imagining of that which is not a cause as having the state of being a cause.

The poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) of a fruit consists in the imagining of something that is not a fruit as being a fruit. Among these three types of *utprekṣā*, the first—*vastūtprekṣā* (fancying a thing)—is twofold: with a stated basis (*uktāspadā*) and with a stated object (*uktaviṣayā*), and with an unstated basis (*anuktāspadā*) and an unstated object (*anuktaviṣayā*). The other two, *hetūtprekṣā* (fancying a cause) and *phalotprekṣā* (fancying a fruit), are each twofold: with an established object (*siddhaviṣayā*) and with an unestablished object (*asiddhaviṣayā*). Thus, there are six varieties of *utprekṣā*.

There is *vastūtprekṣā* (poetic fancy) with an expressed subject, *vastūtprekṣā* with an unexpressed subject, *hetūtprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding cause) with an established subject, *hetūtprekṣā* with an unestablished subject, *phalotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding effect) with an established subject, and *phalotprekṣā* with an unestablished subject. Examples of these are given in order.
*Vastūtprekṣā* with an expressed subject:
"I suspect the mass of darkness to be the smoke of the fires of separation from the female cakravāka birds."

"I suspect this mass of darkness, this thick veil of gloom, to be a mass of smoke from the fires of separation of the female *kokilā* (cakra-vāka) birds; thus, here the object existing at night in the form of darkness is poetically imagined (*utprekṣyate*) as being the very nature of a mass of smoke from the fires of the *kokilā*s' separation. And the grounds for this [imagination] are the connection [of the darkness] with qualities such as blueness and the obstruction of vision."

"I suspect [it is] a mass of smoke and darkness"—since "darkness" is stated as the object (*viṣaya*), this is a *vastūtprekṣā* (poetic fancy based on a real entity). The word "I suspect" (*śaṅke*) is the term that indicates the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). In the same way, words such as *manye*, *dhruvam*, *prāyaḥ*, *nūnam*, and *iva* should also be understood as indicators of poetic fancy.
Here is another example of this very [type]:
"The *palāśa* flowers, curved like the young crescent moon because they had not yet blossomed, shone with an intense redness."
Like nail-marks upon the forest grounds, [these] appeared as soon as they were joined with spring.

Here, because of the connection with qualities such as curvature and redness in the *palāśa* flowers, there arises the imaginative identification (*tādātmya-sambhāvanā*) of them with fresh nail-marks; and since the *viṣaya* (the object of comparison), the *palāśa* flowers, is explicitly mentioned, this is a "poetic fancy of a thing" (*vastūtprekṣā*) with an expressed *viṣaya*.
An example of a "poetic fancy of a thing" with an unexpressed *viṣaya* is:
"The darkness seems to smear the limbs; the sky seems to rain down collyrium. (31)

"Darkness, like a thick gloom, as if smearing the limbs—it performs a smearing upon the limbs"—this is one example. "The sky, like the atmosphere, as if raining collyrium"—this is another example. In both cases, the subject is the pervasion of darkness, yet that [subject] has not been explicitly stated.

And regarding that pervading darkness, by means of its cause—the dense blackening of all objects—there is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) of its identity with the smearing performed by darkness and its identity with the raining of collyrium performed by the sky; thus, it is a *svarūpotprekṣā* (fancy on the nature of a thing) whose object is unstated (*anuktaviṣayā*). Here, the word *iva* indicates probability or supposition.
Another example of this very same [type] is:
"The ocean, as if with the tips of its waves, grinds the sandalwood of foam."
Taking that with his rays, the moon, as it were, anoints the women of the quarters.

Here, the driving forward of the sandalwood foam by the tips of the waves is imagined as its grinding. The spreading of the rays of the moon risen from the ocean across the quarters is imagined as an anointing with sandalwood paste. In the former case, the cause is the massing of the foam at the edge of the ocean; in the latter, the cause is the whitening of the quarters. Since the objects of the two acts—driving and spreading—are not mentioned, these are instances of *vastūtprekṣā* (imagining a thing) with an unstated object (*anuktaviṣayā*).
Poetic fancy regarding a cause (*hetūtprekṣā*) has as its object something already established:

"Your two feet are surely red from being stepped upon on the ground. Here, your two soft feet are "red" (*raktau*), meaning crimson; because of the stepping (*vikṣepaṇāt*)—that is, from walking—on the ground, they are "surely" (*dhruvam*) red. In this case, the stepping on the ground is fancied as the cause of the feet' redness. Since the redness of the feet is already established by nature, stepping is not actually a cause; nevertheless, because there is a possibility of conceiving it as a cause, it is *hetūtprekṣā*.

In this case, the object of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) is the act of casting away, and that [object] is established; since the state of being a cause—or identity with the cause—is fancied with respect to it, this is a "fancy based on a cause" (*hetūtprekṣā*) whose object is established.
Another example of this very same [type] is: "That lord [remained] as if due to the absence of the sun at night and of the moon by day."
He created upon the earth majesty and fame that were ever-risen.

In this [verse], regarding the creation of *pratāpa* (valor) and *yaśas* (fame), the absence of the sun at night and the absence of the moon during the day are inherently established facts; these are here imagined as the causes [of such creation]. Thus, this is a *hetūtprekṣā* (poetic fancy of cause) with a subject that is already established (*siddhaviṣayā*).
An example of *hetūtprekṣā* with an unestablished subject (*asiddhaviṣayā*) is:
"Surely the moon acts as an enemy to the lotuses out of a desire for the splendor of your face. (32)

"The moon, out of a desire to obtain that radiance—the beauty—of your face, engages in enmity with the lotuses. Here, although the opposition between the moon and the lotuses is natural, it is poetically conceived (*utprekṣyate*) as being caused by the moon's desire to attain the splendor of the slender lady’s face. Since the moon’s longing for the beauty of a beloved’s face is not established in reality (i.e., it is non-existent), this is an *utprekṣā* based on a cause whose object is unestablished (*asiddhaviṣaya-hetūtprekṣā*).
Another example of this is:
"The rays of the sun are being mixed together, as it were, by him..."
For people, a thousand cows are equal to a single eye;
since even cows bear the alternative name "eyes," this blindness of theirs is surely due to that, and not to darkness.

The rays of Vivasvat, the Sun, have been mixed with his own beams and led away, as it were, by that eye which is another name for the eyes of people; this blindness is caused by him, not by darkness. Here, the fact that the sun is established as the "eye" of people is a non-established (asiddha) attribute, yet it is poetically imagined (utprekṣita) as the cause of their blindness at night; therefore, this is a "poetic fancy regarding a cause whose object is unestablished" (hetūtprekṣā).
An example of "poetic fancy regarding an effect whose object is established" (siddhaviṣayā phalotprekṣā) is:
"Is this waist bound with golden chains to support its breasts?"

"O beloved! Is this waist—the region between the breasts—bound with golden chains for the sake of supporting or holding them? Here, the encircling of the three folds (valitraya), which is identified as being bound by golden chains, is poetically imagined (utprekṣyate) to have the purpose of supporting the breasts. The waist itself supports the breasts; it is not by the force of the encircling of the three folds—which are identified as being bound by golden chains—that they are held.

And thus, the supporting of the breasts is imagined as the fruit of the binding with golden chains; this is therefore a *phalotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding a result). Furthermore, because the supporting of the breasts is an established fact, it is a *siddhaviṣayā* (one whose object is already accomplished).
Another example of this very same [type] is:
"I suspect that the moon, in order to increase its fullness from the ocean, has taken up many moonstones..."
How many tears does she shed during separation from her beloved, like the eyes of a sorrowful female ruddy goose?

The swelling of the ocean at the rising of the moon is self-evident; nevertheless, it is imagined that the moon causes the moonstone (*candrakāntamaṇi*) to melt and makes tears fall from the eyes of the female *kokila* birds in order to swell the ocean. Thus, the swelling of the ocean is a *phalotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding a result) whose subject is already established, based on the melting of the moonstone and the shedding of tears by the female *kokila*. An example of a *phalotprekṣā* where the subject is not established is as follows:
"The lotus performs penance in the water to attain identity with your foot. (33)

In this verse, the lotus’s natural state of remaining in the water is identified as the "penance of dwelling in water," and the fruit of that penance is then imagined. O beloved! It is likely that the lotus (*abja*) performs the penance of dwelling in water (*udavāsa-tapas*) in order to attain oneness (*aikya*) with your foot; here, the lotus’s natural abiding in the water is identified as penance for the sake of attaining union with the foot of the passionate woman. Thus, the attainment of union with the foot is imagined to be the fruit of the penance of dwelling in water.
Since the attainment of union with the feet of the beloved is already established, this is a *phalotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding the result) whose object is unestablished.
Another example of this very same [figure] is:
"As if for the turning back of the ancient steeds standing upon the chariot..."
The sun set out toward the northern quarter, the birthplace of the best of steeds.

In this instance, the turning around of the ancient horses stationed on the chariot is poetically imagined (*utprekṣyate*) as the result of the sun’s movement toward the northern direction. Since the turning of the horses is not an established fact, this is a *phalotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding a result) whose object is unestablished (*asiddha*). The general definition of this ornament is stated by its very name, *atiśayokti*: it is the expression of an excellence (*atiśaya*), a particularity (*viśeṣa*) that transcends the boundaries of the world (as accepted by poets). Accordingly, Daṇḍin states: "That desire to express a particularity which transcends the limits of the world is *atiśayokti*."

Hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) is of eight kinds: hyperbole of metaphor (*rūpakātiśayokti*), hyperbole of metaphor with concealment (*sāpahnavarūpakātiśayokti*), hyperbole of distinction (*bhedakātiśayokti*), hyperbole of relation (*saṃbandhātiśayokti*), hyperbole of non-relation (*asaṃbandhātiśayokti*), hyperbole of sequencelessness (*akramātiśayokti*), hyperbole of fickleness (*capalātiśayokti*), and absolute hyperbole (*atyantātiśayokti*). The definitions and examples of these are given in order:
Hyperbole of metaphor (*rūpakātiśayokti*) occurs through the identification [of one thing] after having swallowed [its own identity].
Behold, cold arrows are emerging from the pair of blue lotuses.

Having "swallowed" (nigīrya)—that is, having grasped the object by means of the word denoting the subject itself without employing a word for the object itself—there would be *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) due to the determination (*adhyavasāna*) of the object in the form of the subject, arising from an imposed conviction (*āhāryaniścaya*). "Imposedness" (*āhāryatva*) consists in being produced by a desire existing at the time of sublation (*bādhakālīna*).

The essential conclusion is this: where the object of comparison (*upameya*), such as the face, is not expressed by its own denotative term (e.g., "face") but is instead expressed solely by terms denoting the standard of comparison (*upamāna*)—such as the moon—and is thereby determined as being of the nature of that [standard] (either through identity with or similarity to the moon), there lies the figure *rūpakātiśayokti* (hyperbole of metaphor). For example: "O friend! From the pair of blue lotuses, sharp arrows are issuing forth. In this instance, the eyes are not called "eyes" but are instead identified as "blue lotuses," from which "sharp arrows" (tears) emerge.

Here, without employing words that directly denote the objects—the pair of glances from the beloved who is the object of perception—one employs instead the words "blue lotus" (*nīlotpala*) and "arrow" (*śara*), which denote the subjects; thus, through the identification (*adhyavasāna*) of the pair of blue lotuses with the pair of arrows, there is the figure of speech known as *rūpakātiśayokti* (hyperbole of metaphor).

The distinction between these two is as follows: in *rūpaka* (metaphor), there is the apprehension of identity between the object (*viṣaya*) and the subject (*viṣayin*), both of which are expressed by their own respective words; however, in *rūpakātiśayokti* (hyperbole of metaphor), there is no expression of the object by its own word, but rather the object is expressed only by the term denoting the subject, resulting in a superimposed determination of identity (*adhyavasāya*). Furthermore, in *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), there is merely a possibility of identity, not a certainty.
In *bhrānti* (error), the apprehension of identity is not superimposed, but is instead produced by a misapprehension of something else. Thus should the distinction be understood.
Here is another example of *rūpakātiśayokti*:
A certain pond shines in the sky; beyond that, one has reached a golden flight of stairs with a subtle path made of sapphires.
Ahead are two mountains, easy for the virtuous to traverse, their regions covered in sandalwood trees.
For those residing there, nectar is easily obtained due to the proximity of the moon.

Here, by means of words denoting the standards of comparison (*upamāna*)—such as "pond," "sky," and "delicate lotus"—the objects of comparison (*upameya*), namely the navel, the waist, and the line of body hair, are swallowed up and identified with the forms of the pond and so forth; thus, this is *rūpakātiśayokti* (hyperbole of metaphor).
This is considered *sāpahnavā rūpakātiśayokti* (metaphorical hyperbole involving concealment) when it contains the essence of *apahnuti* (concealment).
Specifically, that very same [figure] is regarded as *sāpahnavā* when it possesses the nature of being pregnant with concealment.
O King, those who are deluded perceive nectar in your eloquent verses as being in the moon.

If that very same *rūpakātiśayokti* (hyperbole of metaphor) is characterized by concealment—that is, constructed with a negation—then it is considered and called *sāpahnavā rūpakātiśayokti* (hyperbole of metaphor with concealment). O King, in your eloquent sayings (*sūkti*), which are sweet words, there exists nectar (*sudhā*)—this is the ellipsis. Deluded, ignorant, or even mad people perceive or know that nectar to be in the moon (*vidhu*). The underlying sense is that, in reality, there is no nectar in the moon.

Here, because there is an identification (*adhyavasāna*) of the sweetness of the poetic utterance with nectar (*sudhā*), and because it contains a negation—namely, that "there is no nectar in the moon"—it is *rūpakātiśayokti* (hyperbole of metaphor) with concealment (*sāpahnavā*).
Another example of this very same figure is: "Between pearl and coral, the sweet juice [of the flower]; the flower alone bears the heavy burden..."
Indeed, the single abode of those two [the moon and the sun] is not in the ocean, but rather in the orb of the moon;
it rises upon the summit of Mount Śaṅkha and not within the eastern mountain range— such are the distinctions made by those for whom she is not within the path of vision.

In this case, between the pearl (*muktā*) and the coral (*vidruma*), there is "sweet juice" (*madhurasa*); however, the "juice of flowers" (*puṣparasas*) is not the "sweet juice. The pearl and the coral reside in the lunar orb (*candramaṇḍala*), but not in the ocean; and the moon rises from the crest of a conch (*śaṅkhaśiras*), not from the slopes of the eastern mountain (*pūrvādri*). In such instances, the words *muktā*, *vidruma*, *madhurasa*, *candramaṇḍala*, and *śaṅkha*—along with *adhara*, *adharamādhurya*, *mukha*, and *kaṇṭha*—are swallowed up (negated) and superimposed (*adhyavasita*) in the form of the pearl and so forth.

In the verse beginning with "The flower is the supreme bearer of burdens" (puṣpaṃ paraṃ dhūrvaham), since negations such as "the nectar of the flower is not the nectar of wine" are implied, this is *rūpakātiśayokti* (hyperbole of metaphor) with concealment (*sāpahnavā*).
Exaggeration by way of distinction (bhedakātiśayokti):
Exaggeration by way of distinction occurs when that very thing is described as being otherwise.
"The profundity of this lord of the earth is one thing indeed; his fortitude is another. (36)

When there is a description of difference regarding a quality such as profundity (*gāmbhīrya*) of that very object well-known in the world—even though there is no actual difference—it is "Hyperbole of Differentiation" (*bhedakātiśayokti*). In the statement, "The profundity of this lord of the earth is indeed different; his fortitude too is different—truly distinct from that of the world," although profundity and fortitude are common to the world (i.e., despite the absence of difference), their distinctness (i.e., difference) is described; thus, it is *bhedakātiśayokti*. Another example of this same [figure] is:
"This perfection of beauty is one thing; the range of her cleverness is another."
This lotus-petal-eyed woman is no ordinary creation of the Creator.

Here, although there is no difference in the perfection of form and other qualities as established in the world, a difference is described; thus, this is *bhedakātiśayokti* (hyperbole of distinction). *Saṃbandhātiśayokti* (hyperbole of relation) occurs when a relation is imagined where none exists.
The tops of the palaces of this city touch the orb of the moon.

When there is a lack of connection—that is, in the absence of a relation—the conceptualization of a connection, the description of a relation, is *sambandhātiśayokti* (hyperbole of relation).
