For example: "The tops of the palaces, the peaks of the mansions of this city, touch the orb of the moon. Here, although the lofty palace peaks are in reality incapable of touching the lunar orb, because their contact with it is described, this is *sambandhātiśayokti*. Another illustration of this very same figure is:
"In a few days, the Golden Mountain (Meru) would reach its end, having brought its day to a close."
Thus the female ruddy goose (cakravākī) experiences joy while King Vīrarudradeva is characterized by his liberality.

Here, although there is no actual connection between the female ruddy goose and the satisfaction arising from the apprehension of the destruction of Mount Kanaka—Mahāmeru, the cause of the sun’s setting—the description of such a connection constitutes *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) based on a [non-existent] relation.
This is *asaṃbandhātiśayokti* (hyperbole of non-connection).
"Union is called non-union because of the absence of connection;
O Indra among kings, since you are the giver, we pay no heed to the celestial trees."

When there is a connection, the description of a lack of connection—that is, non-connection—is called *asaṃbandhātiśayokti* (hyperbole of non-connection). O King of kings! while you, the giver, are present and distinguished by your generosity, we do not honor nor do we beg from the celestial trees (*svardruma*, i.e., the wish-fulfilling trees)—this is the example. Here, even though the king is of a generous nature, everyone naturally has regard for the celestial trees; nevertheless, despite the presence of such regard, the conceptualization of non-regard through the phrase "we do not honor" constitutes *asaṃbandhātiśayokti*. An example of its boundless variety follows:
O lady of faultless limbs, as these two breasts expand, there is no sufficient space within the interval of your vine-like arms.

In this case, although there is sufficient space between the two swelling breasts within the space of the arms, the description of their lack of connection by stating "it is not sufficient" even when such a connection exists constitutes *asambandhātiśayokti* (hyperbole of non-connection).
*Akramātiśayokti* (hyperbole of non-succession) occurs when cause and effect exist simultaneously.
O King, your arrows and bowstrings alike embrace one another as they fly toward the enemy.

The definition of *akramātiśayokti* (simultaneity of non-sequential order) is as follows: when the coexistence or simultaneity (*yaugapadya*) of cause and effect (*hetu-kārya*) is described. This means that by transgressing the rule that "the cause must precede and the effect follow immediately," the description of cause and effect as occurring at the same time constitutes *akramātiśayokti*. For example: "O King! Your arrows and your enemies simultaneously (*samaṃ yugapat*) embrace the bowstring and the earth. In this instance, the arrows (cause) and the enemies (effect) are both depicted as embracing the bowstring (cause) and the earth (effect) at one and the same moment.

In this instance, although there exists a temporal sequence between the cause—the fixing of the arrow upon the bowstring—and the effect—the falling of the enemies to the ground, their simultaneity is described; thus, this is the figure of speech known as *akramātiśayokti* (hyperbole of non-sequentiality).
Another example of this is:
"The host of enemies releases its treasury and undergoes trembling."
As soon as the sword of the hero Hammīra is cast down, he quickly abandons his forbearance.

In this context, regarding the sword of the hero Hammīra: as soon as it leaves its sheath (*kośa*), the host of enemies immediately abandons their treasury (*kośa*); as soon as the sword trembles, the enemies likewise tremble. Because of this description of the simultaneity of cause and effect, there is the figure of speech *akramātiśayokti*.
As for *capalātiśayokti*:
"But *capalātiśayokti* occurs when the effect arises from the occurrence of a cause."
When the slender woman uttered the words "yasyāmī" (in whom I am), her bracelets became bracelets of sorrow (dur-mikā).

When the effect is described as being produced by the mere cognition of the cause—that is, by the mere awareness of the cause—the poetic figure is *cāpala-atiśayokti* (exaggeration of fickleness). For example, when the hero says, "I shall go," meaning "I will depart for a distant land," the slender heroine’s ring, finger-ring, bracelet, or hand-ornament becomes [the very essence of] the knowledge of separation (*viraha-jñāna*) merely through that awareness. This is the illustration.

Here, because the emaciation of the slender lady has arisen from the mere knowledge of the cause of her future separation—since the ring has become a hand-ornament—this description of the production of an effect constitutes the *capalātiśayokti* (hyperbole of fickleness).
Another example of this is:
"Even when a flower was seen but once, the tip of the hand became blood-red to grasp it..."
Even the rumor of dyeing with lac suddenly reddens the soles of her feet;
even the mere memory of applying ointment to her limbs brings inner distress; alas, for this woman of unsteady gaze, what else could even the fragrance of her hair not become a burden?

Here, in the case of a heroine naturally delicate who, during her state of separation, desires to gather [flowers], her hand becomes red in a mere moment from grasping the flower; likewise, even by the report of lac-dye, the soles of her feet become red. Because the production of the effect is described here through the mere occurrence of the cause, this is *capalātiśayokti* (hyperbole of fickleness). Another example of this very same figure is as follows:
"Shall I go? Shall I not go?"—as the husband speaks thus before her, in an instant, the slender-limbed woman... [becomes pale].
The bracelets on the forearms have slipped off, and likewise, others have been shattered.

In this case, by the mere possibility (*prasakti*) of the two states—separation and its absence—the two effects, namely emaciation and corpulence, arise simultaneously. Through these effects, it is described that the loosening of the girdle in front and the bursting of others [the hips] occur at the same time. Thus, the distinction here is that even for two effects produced by the possibility of causes, their simultaneity is depicted. This is *atyantātiśayokti* (hyperbole of extreme excess), which occurs when there is a transposition of temporal sequence (*paurvāparyavyatikrama*).
Her pride departed first, and afterwards she was conciliated by her beloved.

*Atyantātiśayokti* (hyperbole of extreme excellence) occurs when there is a transgression—that is, a violation—of the sequence of priority and posteriority between cause and effect. The meaning is that by overstepping the established order in which the cause precedes and the effect follows, the description of the occurrence of the cause immediately after the production of the effect constitutes *atyantātiśayokti*.

In this case, pride—that is, the anger of love—departed first, and afterwards the heroine was conciliated by her beloved. Since the effect, the abandonment of pride, is described as having arisen even before the well-known cause, namely the act of conciliation, this is an illustration of *atyantātiśayokti* (hyperbole consisting of the inversion of the sequence between cause and effect). Another example of this very same [figure] is: "O friend, the courtyards of the great poets became [filled with them] even earlier..."
Sweet with the fragrance of ichor from the elephants agitated by contact with hovering bees—
these glances of King Rudra fall upon them from behind, like companions to the vast waves surging from the Ocean of Milk.

Here, first the courtyards of the poets were filled by King Rudra’s elephants; thereafter, the king’s glances fell upon the poets. Because this describes the falling of the glances—the cause—immediately after the giving of the elephants—the effect—it constitutes an *atyantātiśayokti* (hyperbole of extreme excess). In this regard, it should be noted that the final three figures—*akramacapalā*, *capalā*, and *atyantātiśayokti*—are based on the sequence of cause and effect and manifest the swiftness of the action.

*Tulyayogitā* (Equal Pairing) is the state of being connected by a single attribute among things that are equal, meaning those possessing similarity. It is fourfold: consisting of the connection of a single attribute with the subjects under discussion (*prastuta*), consisting of the connection of a single attribute with things not under discussion (*aprastuta*), consisting of the equality of conduct regarding the beneficial and the harmful, and consisting of the statement of equating the superior. The definitions and examples for these are given in order.
Regarding the first and second types of *tulyayogitā*: "Tulyayogitā is the unity of attribute between the objects of description or others."
The lotuses close their petals, as do the faces of wanton women.

The figure of speech *tulyayogitā* (Equal Pairing) consists in the unity of attributes—that is, the connection with a single attribute in the form of a quality or action—among either those things being described (*prastuta*) alone, or else among others that are not being described (*aprastuta*). The conclusion is this: where the connection with a single attribute is described between two things that are both being described, or among many things that are all being described, there is the first type of *tulyayogitā*. Where the connection with a single attribute exists among two or many things that are all not being described, there is the second type of *tulyayogitā*.

In the root text, the plural form in both instances—"of the subjects" (*varṇyānām*) and "of the others" (*itareṣām*)—is employed with the intention of denoting plurality. Thus, the definition of the first type of *tulyayogitā* is the state of possessing a single attribute connected solely to multiple subjects (*prastuta*), while the definition of the second is the state of possessing a single attribute connected solely to multiple non-subjects (*aprastuta*).

"The lotuses (*sarojāni*) and the faces (*vadanāni*) of the independent women (*svairiṇīnām*) who go to meet their lovers (*abhisārikāṇām*) both contract and undergo closure"—this is an example of *prastutatulyayogitā* (the figure of "Equal Pairing" involving the subject under description). At the rising of the moon, the lotuses contract and close; and the faces of the independent women contract out of fear of the light. Thus, because the described lotuses and the faces of the independent women are connected to the single action of contracting, this constitutes *prastutatulyayogitā*.
"In whose heart does it not appear [as beautiful] when the softness of your limbs is seen?"
The harshness of the *mālatī* flower, the crescent moon, and the plantain tree!

"O beloved! When the softness of your limbs is beheld, in whose conscious heart would the hardness of the *mālatī* flower, the crescent moon, and the plantain tree not appear? This is an example of *aprastutatulyayogitā* (similarity of the irrelevant). Here, while the description of the heroine’s tenderness is the relevant subject (*prastuta*), the description of the hardness—a single shared quality—of the irrelevant (*aprastuta*) *mālatī*, the moon’s digit, and the plantain tree constitutes *aprastutatulyayogitā*. Other examples of the first and second types of *tulyayogitā* follow.

The days attained growth as they bore a profusion of blossoms accompanied by emerging petals, clearly turning crimson from the touch of the sun's rays; and the lotuses, opening wide, likewise flourished.

In this description of summer, the days and the lotuses are the subjects; since they both attain growth through contact with the rays of the sun, there is *prastutatulyayogitā* (parallelism of the relevant), because a single action—the attainment of growth—is attributed to the subjects alone. The trunks of the lordly elephants, due to their roughness to the touch, and the excellent plantain trees, due to their extreme coolness—even though they have attained a full and expansive form in the world, they have become excluded from being similes for her thighs.

In this description of the thighs, the elephant’s trunk and the specific plantain trees (*kadalī*) are irrelevant subjects (*aprastuta*). Since they fall outside the range of possible similes for the thighs, there occurs an *aprastutatulyayogitā* (irrelevant parallelism), because these irrelevant elements—the elephant’s trunks and the specific plantain trees—are described as sharing a single common attribute: being excluded from the category of suitable similes.
The third type of *tulyayogitā* is the equality of conduct toward both the beneficial and the harmful; this is another form of *tulyayogitā*.
Defeat is being bestowed by you upon both friend and foe. ||44||

*Tulyayogitā* (Equal Treatment) is another [figure], the third kind, consisting of the equality, similarity, or uniform treatment of action (*vṛtti*) regarding what is beneficial and what is harmful, or regarding friend and foe. O King! "By you, in the matter of friends and enemies (*mitrebhyaḥ śatrubhyaśca*), both supreme prosperity (*parābhūtiḥ*—the prefix *parā-* here meaning *parā utkṛṣṭā bhūtiḥ*, i.e., pre-eminent sovereignty) and defeat (*parābhavaḥ*) are bestowed"—this is the example. Here, because there is a description of a common activity in the form of bestowing "defeat" upon both the friend who is beneficial and the enemy who is harmful, it is *tulyayogitā*.
There is an equality [of the two acts] due to the identification (adhyavasāna) through punning (śleṣa) between the giving of supreme prosperity and the giving of defeat.
Another example of this very same [figure] is:
"He who [cuts] the neem tree with an axe, and he who [waters] it with honey and ghee..."
And whoever offers this [the body] perfumes, garlands, and so forth, he is bitter to everyone.

In this context, the verbal forms *vṛścati* (cuts), *siñcati* (sprinkles), and *arcati* (worships) are to be supplied. Because the neem tree is harmful when subjected to cutting with an axe, yet beneficial when honored with honey, ghee, perfumes, garlands, and so forth—and because it is described as being equally pungent in both cases—the figure of speech *tulyayogitā* (Equal Treatment) applies due to the description of a common operation. The distinction is that the previous example culminates in the praise of the king, whereas this one culminates in the censure of the neem tree.
This is the fourth type of *tulyayogitā*; another type of *tulyayogitā* consists of speech that equalizes things by virtue of their superior qualities.
Yama the world-protector, Varuṇa the wielder of the noose, Kubera the giver of fortune, Śakra, and you yourself as well.

Having equated—meaning having made equal or established a similarity—with those preeminent in their groups by means of superior qualities such as heroism, the description or statement is another type of *tulyayogitā* (Equal Pairing). The meaning is that another *tulyayogitā* consists of a description made by equating [the subject] with others through superior qualities by way of their common attribute (*dharma*).

In the example: "Yama, Varuṇa the wielder of the noose, Kubera the giver of wealth, Śakra the Indra, and you too are a world-protector (*lokapāla*)," the king who is the subject of description is described by equating him with Yama and the others through superior qualities by way of the common attribute of being a world-protector; thus the definition is fulfilled.
Another example of this is:
"The glances of deer-eyed women and flashes of lightning—
though initiated by clouds themselves— do not endure for even two moments."

Here, because the gatherings of women and the flashes of lightning do not remain for even two moments, there is a connection with the definition of *tulyayogitā* (parallelism), as the union with fawn-eyed women is presented as being equalized with the flashes of lightning through the common property (*dharmatā*) of not persisting for two moments. The distinction is that the previous example culminates in praise, whereas this one culminates in censure. Scholars define *dīpaka* (the illuminator) as the unification of the attribute of things both described and not described: "The young elephant shines with rut; the lord of the earth shines with his majesty. (16)

The wise declare that *dīpaka* (the Illuminator) is the connection of a single attribute (*ekadharmānvaya*) among both the described (*varṇya*) and the undescribed (*avarṇya*), or the relevant (*prastuta*) and the irrelevant (*aprastuta*). It should be understood here that the plural number in "described and undescribed" (*varṇyāvarṇyānām*) is intended to signify more than one. Thus, the definition is: *dīpaka* is a single attribute shared by both the described and the undescribed. The distinction from *tulyayogitā* (Equal Pairing) is this: in *tulyayogitā*, there is a connection with a single attribute either among the described alone, or among the undescribed alone; whereas in *dīpaka*, it is among both the described and the undescribed.

"A young elephant (*kalabhaḥ*), a young male elephant (*karikalabhaḥ*), shines (*bhāti*) with rut; a lord of the earth (*mahīpatiḥ*) shines with majesty and valor"—this is the example. Here, the connection to the single action of "shining" is described for both the subject of description, the king, and the subject not being described, the young elephant; thus, the application of the definition is established. Similarity is implied here.

A quality (*dharma*) employed because of its utility for the subject at hand (in this case, the form of *bhāna*) may also be useful for what is not the subject; just as a lamp lit for the purpose of illuminating a house also illuminates the street, it is called *dīpaka* based on its similarity to a lamp—a name whose meaning is consistent with its function. The suffix *kan* is added in the sense of "like" (*iva*), as in *dīpa iva dīpakam*.
Another example of *dīpaka* is:
"The gem polished on the whetstone, the victor in battle crushed by weapons..."
An elephant with its rut exhausted, a river in autumn with its sandy banks dried up,
the moon with but a single digit remaining, a young woman worn out by lovemaking—
these shine with a beauty born of emaciation; so too do kings who have lost their wealth when it comes to supplicants.

In this context, kings whose wealth has vanished when suppliants arrive, and gems and the like that have been ground on a whetstone, both shine through their diminished state; thus, because there is a description of the connection with a single common attribute—namely, "shining"—between the subjects under discussion (the kings) and the non-subjects (the gems and so forth), there is a correspondence with the definition of the *dīpaka* figure.
Regarding the *āvṛttidīpaka* ornament:
"The *āvṛttidīpaka* occurs when the *dīpaka* is repeated in three ways."

Because a lamp serves many purposes, when there is a repetition of the word, the sense, or both—which stand in the place of a lamp—the *āvṛttidīpaka* (lamp of repetition) becomes threefold: *padāvṛttidīpaka* (repetition of the word), *arthāvṛttidīpaka* (repetition of the sense), and *padārthobhayāvṛttidīpaka* (repetition of both word and sense). Examples of these are given in order.
An example of *padāvṛttidīpaka* is:
"This garland of clouds rains, and this night rains as well. (47)

"This garland of clouds, this row of rain-clouds, rains and releases water; and this night also rains, acting like a year"—here, because of the power of *śleṣa* (punning), the word "rains" (*varṣati*), which is capable of assisting both the relevant (*prakṛta*) and the irrelevant (*aprakṛta*) subjects, is repeated in two sentences; since the meanings are distinct, this is *padāvṛttidīpaka* (the illuminator through the repetition of a word).

Because these are the words of a woman separated from her lover, it is appropriate that the night seems like a year; however, in reality, the definition of *dīpaka* (illumination) does not apply here, since both the "garland of clouds" and the "night" are the subjects under discussion (*prakṛta*). Therefore, the ornament is simply *āvṛtti* (repetition), which is designated as *āvṛttidīpaka* because it possesses the shadow of *dīpaka*.
Here is another example of this:
"The garland of clouds excites the longing of the flocks of peacocks."
And today, the god whose banner is the sea-monster agitates the minds of young men with longing.

In this instance, the "garland of clouds" (*meghamālā*) causes the flock of peacocks to yearn (*utkaṇṭhayati*), making their necks erect; meanwhile, the "one whose banner is the sea-monster" (*makaradhvaja*, i.e., the god of love) causes the minds of youths to yearn (*utkaṇṭhayati*), making them eager. Since there is a difference in meaning (*arthabheda*), this is *padāvṛttidīpaka* (the lamp of word-repetition).
An example of *arthāvṛttidīpaka* (the lamp of meaning-repetition) is as follows:
"The *kadamba* flowers bloom; the *kuṭaja* trees burst open."

The *kadamba* trees—meaning *kadamba* flowers—are blossoming (*unmīlanti*), and the *kuṭaja* trees—meaning *girimallikā*—are blooming (*sphuṭanti*). Here, despite the difference between the two words, because the meaning "blooming" is repeated, this is *arthāvṛttidīpaka* (repetition of the sense). Another example of this very same [figure] is: "The stream from the clouds pacifies the thirst of the young *cātaka* birds that has persisted for a long time."
And the stream of tears from the eyes of the young wives dries up the sorrow born of travel for lovers.

Here, although there is a difference between the two words *śapayati* and *kṣapayati*, there is a repetition of a single meaning; thus, this is an instance of *arthāvṛttidīpaka* (the illuminator through the repetition of meaning).
An example of *śabdārthobhayāvṛttidīpaka* (the illuminator through the repetition of both word and meaning) is as follows: "The cātaka birds rejoice, satisfied, and the peacocks also rejoice. (48)

The *cātakas* are intoxicated—meaning they become thrilled and exhilarated—by drinking the water of the clouds; and the peacocks (*śikhāvalas*) are intoxicated—meaning they become thrilled and exhilarated—by the sight of the clouds and by hearing their thundering. Here, because the word *mādyanti* and its secondary meaning of "overflowing" are both repeated, this is an instance of *dīpaka* (illumination) occurring through the repetition of both sound and sense. Another example of this very same [type] is: "Defeated by your face, the orb of the moon hides itself within the cloud."
And even the lotus, O beautiful one! sinks into the flood of waters.

Here, the orb of the moon, defeated by the face of Sundarī, hides—meaning it becomes invisible—in the cloud; and the lotus hides—meaning it becomes invisible—in the flood of waters. Because of the recurrence of the word *nilīyate* and the recurrence of its meaning, namely concealment (*tirodhāna*), this is an instance of *dīpaka* involving the recurrence of both word and meaning. When there is a single common attribute between two sentences, it is considered *prativastūpamā* (simile by parallelism): “The sun shines with heat; the hero shines with his bow.”

When there is a single commonality (*ekasāmānya*)—that is, when there is a connection with a single common attribute (*samānadharmānvaya*) that is separately specified—in the two sentences, namely the sentence containing the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the sentence containing the object of comparison (*upameya*), *prativastūpamā* is considered or observed. The essential point is that where a single common attribute belonging to the two sentences composed of the standard and object of comparison is indicated separately by means of different words, that is *prativastūpamā*.

*Prativastūpamā* (the simile based on corresponding objects) is an ornament whose name is literal (*anvarthanāman*), derived from the etymology: "that in which there is a common property (*samānadharmā*) for every object (*prati-vastu*) and every sentence-meaning (*prati-vākyārtha*). For example: "The sun (*sūraḥ*) shines (*bhrājate*) with heat (*tāpena*)," and "the hero (*śūraḥ*), a brave man, shines (*rājate*) with his bow (*cāpena*). Here, by means of two different words—*bhrājate* and *rājate*—the single common property of "shining" (*prakāśana-rūpa*) is indicated in two sentences composed of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*). In this case, the sun is the *upamāna* and the hero is the *upameya*.
Another example of *prativastūpamā*:
The steady character of the virtuous is not disturbed by the intellect of the wicked;
for the flame of a jewel-lamp is not extinguished even by a gale.

The style is excellent. "Ratnadīpa" means a lamp that is itself a jewel. The first half-verse is the sentence containing the object of comparison (*upameya*), and the second half-verse is the sentence containing the standard of comparison (*upamāna*). Since the common attribute (*samānadharma*)—the absence of destruction—is presented in both cases through different words, there is a formal correspondence with the definition of *prativastūpamā* (parallelism).
If there is a relationship of prototype and reflection (*bimbapratibimba*), that is the ornament *dṛṣṭānta* (illustration).
"O King, you alone are possessed of fame; for the moon alone is possessed of splendor. (50)

The term "of two sentences" (*vākyayoḥ*) is understood to carry over [from the previous definition]. If there is the relationship of prototype and reflection (*bimbapratibimbatva*) between two sentences—that is, between the sentence expressing the object of comparison (*upameya*) and the sentence expressing the standard of comparison (*upamāna*)—and if two distinct attributes, having been determined as non-different due to their similarity, are indicated separately, then that is the figure of speech *Dṛṣṭānta* (Exemplification). An example is: "O King, you alone possess fame; the moon alone possesses luster. Here, the first is the sentence of the object of comparison, and the second is the sentence of the standard of comparison.

The two properties—fame (*kīrti*) and beauty (*kānti*)—belonging to those two [the moon and the face] are indicated as being in the relation of the original (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*); such is the application of the definition.

In reality, the separate mention of two properties that are distinct yet determined to be non-distinct due to their similarity constitutes the *bimbapratibimbabhāva*. In reality, the separate employment of what is essentially one and the same property through different words constitutes the *vastuprativastubhāva*. Thus, the distinction between these two is that the *vastuprativastubhāva* occurs in the *prativastūpamā*, whereas the *bimbapratibimbabhāva* occurs in the *dṛṣṭānta*.
Another illustration of this example:

"Granted, there may be thousands of other kings; yet they say the earth possesses a true king only because of him. Though crowded with constellations, stars, and planets, the night is radiant only by means of the moon."

In this context, the figure of speech is *dṛṣṭānta* (illustration) based on the relationship between the original image (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*), because in the two sentences—"this earth is *rājanvatī* (possessing a noble king) by means of this king"—and "the night is *jyotiṣmatī* (radiant) by means of the moon," or "endowed with excellent light"—two distinct yet similar attributes, namely *rājanvatī* and *jyotiṣmatī*, are mentioned separately.

*Nidarśanā* (poetic illustration) is of three kinds: functioning through the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārthavṛtti*), functioning through the meaning of a word (*padārthavṛtti*), and consisting in the communication of an existing or non-existing fact (*sadasadarthabodhanarūpā*). Their definitions and examples are given in order.
First, *vākyārthavṛtti-nidarśanā*:
Nidarśanā (Illustration) is the superimposition of identity between two similar things, as in:
"That gentleness of the donor is indeed the spotlessness of the full moon. (51)

*Nidarśanā* (illustration) is the superimposition of identity (*aikyāropa*)—that is, the superimposition of non-difference (*abhedāropa*)—between two sentence-meanings (*vākyārtha*) that are similar or equal. It functions at the level of the sentence meaning. For example: "That which is the gentleness—the lack of harshness—of a donor who is disposed to giving, this is the spotlessness—the state of being free from blemish—of the full moon. The sense is that just as the spotlessness of the full moon is inconceivable, so too is the gentleness of a donor difficult to find. The word *yat* is neuter in gender because it refers to a general quality; the word *seyam* ("this very one") is feminine in gender because it intends to designate the subject (*vidheya*).

Here, because there is an imposition of identity—by means of the words *yat* and *tat*—between the meaning of the sentence containing the object of comparison (the donor), characterized by his lack of harshness, and the meaning of the sentence containing the standard of comparison (the full moon), characterized by its freedom from blemish, this is *nidarśanā* (illustrative identification) residing in the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). The distinction is that in a *rūpaka* (metaphor), there is an imposition of identity between the mere standard of comparison and the object of comparison, whereas in *nidarśanā*, there is an imposition of identity between two sentence-meanings composed of the standard of comparison and the object of comparison. Furthermore, the distinction is that in a *dṛṣṭānta* (simile), there is a presentation of two similar sentence-meanings through the relationship of prototype and reflection (*bimba-pratibimba-bhāva*), whereas in *nidarśanā*, there is an imposition of oneness.
Another example for the purpose of illustrating the repetition of a sentence is as follows:
"Weeping has been done in the forest; the body of a corpse has been anointed with unguents; a lotus has been planted on dry land; and rain has been poured for a long time upon barren soil."
The ignorant person who has been served is like one who bends down to stroke a dog's tail, whispers into the ear of a deaf man, or holds up a mirror before the face of a blind man.

In this context, in such passages as "The service rendered by an ignorant person here is like weeping in a forest," there is a superimposition of non-difference (*abheda-āropa*) between the meaning of the sentence expressing the object of comparison—the service of an ignorant person—and the meanings of the sentences expressing the standards of comparison—weeping in a forest and so forth. The intended sense is that the service of an ignorant person is as fruitless as weeping in a forest. Some maintain that there is another variety of *nidarśanā* (illustration) which functions at the level of word-meanings (*padārtha-vṛtti*).
Your pair of eyes bears the grace of two blue lotuses.

Some authorities state that there is another variety of *nidarśanā* consisting of the superimposition (*āropa*) of the attributes of one object onto a single object. For example: "(O beloved,) your pair of eyebrows—that is, your two eyes—bears the grace (*vilāsa*), meaning the charm, of blue lotuses (*nīlāmbujanman*), i.e., blue water-lilies. This is the illustrative instance.

Here, since there is a superimposition (*āropa*) upon the pair of the beloved’s eyes of that quality belonging to the compound object—the pair of blue lotuses—which consists of *vilāsa* (graceful charm), this is *padārthavṛttinidarśanā*. In this case, the quality being superimposed is conveyed by the word itself; thus it is called *padārthavṛtti* (functioning at the level of the word). Since the grace of the blue lotus is impossible in the eyes, the superimposition—by implying a similar quality through the phrase "grace like grace"—results ultimately in a simile (*aupamya*).

The distinction between these two is as follows: *vākyārthavṛttinidarśanā* is the superimposition of identity between two distinct attributes, whereas *padārthavṛttinidarśanā* is the superimposition of the attributes of one object onto another, either the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) or the object compared (*upameya*).
Another example of *padārthavṛttinidarśanā* is:
"The paleness upon the cheeks of the women of Gauḍa during separation..."
He was seen amidst the dust within the clusters of thorny shrubs.

Here, because the quality of another—namely, the paleness of the cheeks of Gauda women—is superimposed upon a different object, namely, the pollen within the clusters of *rājajambū* blossoms, this is *padārthavṛttinidarśanā* (illustration residing in an object). The distinction is that in the previous example there was a superimposition of the qualities of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) onto the object of comparison (*upameya*), whereas here there is a superimposition of the qualities of the object of comparison onto the standard of comparison. Even here, since the quality of one thing is impossible in another, it culminates in a simile by implying a quality similar to it.
They say that *nidarśanā* consists in the communication of a real or unreal meaning;
others define it as the communication of an unreal or a real meaning through an action.

When, through an action—specifically the action of someone characterized by some particular act—one informs or makes known to others the non-existent and the existent meanings, namely, the non-existent result of a fault or the existent result of a quality while it is being described, they call this another, distinct type of *nidarśanā* different from the previous one. Thus, this too is twofold: that which consists in making known a non-existent meaning through an action, and that which consists in making known an existent meaning through an action. It is called *nidarśanā* because it "shows" (*nidarśayati*) or demonstrates [the meaning] by means of an action.
An example of *nidarśanā* consisting in making known a non-existent meaning through an action is as follows:
"May the opponent of the king perish, like darkness at the rising of the moon when it has been exhausted. (53)

"An adversary of the king shall perish; he shall meet with destruction"—thus [the speaker] informs others. In the statement, "At the rising of the moon, the darkness has waned and vanished," because the result of the fault—the unreal meaning—is communicated through the metaphorical action of the waning of darkness at the moon's rise—namely, that "an adversary of the king shall perish"—there is a formal application of the definition [of *dhvani*]. Through the wordplay (*śleṣa*) on the word "king" (*rājan*), there is the simultaneous apprehension of both the monarch and the moon.
Another example of this very same [type of *dhvani*] is:
"He who, having attained a high position, is base, will surely fall with ease."
A herd of spotted deer, situated upon a mountain peak and shaken by a pleasant breeze, falls downward.

In this context, if a drop of rain situated on a mountain peak, rendered light by a mere gentle breeze, ascends to a higher position, then the realization of an unreal state through effortless downward action [is illustrated]. An example of *nidarśanā* (illustration), which consists of the realization of a real state through action, is as follows:
"The sun, even as it rises, bestows its splendor upon the lotus."
Reflecting that the fruit of all prosperities is the favoring of one's friends. || 54 ||

Savitṛ, the Sun, while rising—that is, while attaining his very emergence—manifesting prosperity, success, and the fruit of abundance as "favor to friends," bestows splendor and beauty upon the lotuses, who are his own friends. Here, by means of the action consisting of the bestowing of splendor upon the lotuses, the Sun conveys to others a beneficial meaning: "Just as I do, so may another also grant prosperity to friends at the time of their own rising. Because of this description, which consists of making known a virtuous matter, it is *nidarśanā* (illustrative representation). Another example of this same figure follows.
He placed the god Ravi, who had arrived, upon the position of his crest-jewel,
thereby instructing householders that hospitality must be extended to the virtuous.

In this instance, because the description conveys a meaningful truth—that the Udayagiri mountain, by its own action of bearing the sun upon its head when he arrives at dawn, teaches householders that they must perform hospitality for guests—it is an example of *nidarśanā* (illustrative simile) consisting of the communication of a significant meaning.
*Vyatireka* (contrast) occurs when there is a distinction between the object of comparison and the standard of comparison:
"Though they are as lofty as mountains, they are by nature tender. (55)

If the distinction or difference (*vailakṣaṇya*) between the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameya*) is described, it is the figure of speech *vyatireka* (distinction). The virtuous (*santaḥ*), like mountains (*śailāḥ*), are lofty; [mountains are lofty in form, while the virtuous are lofty in character]. However, [the virtuous] are by nature (*prakṛtyā*) tender and soft, whereas [mountains are hard]—this is the intended sense. Here, the phrase "tender by nature" describes the distinction of the subjects of comparison, the virtuous, from the objects of comparison, the mountains; thus, the definition of *vyatireka* is fully applicable.

*Vyatireka* means distinction (*vailakṣaṇya*). This results, depending on the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), either in the superiority, inferiority, or equality of the object compared (*upameya*). In this instance, it culminates in the exaltation of the object compared. Another example of *sahokti* (concomitance) is as follows:
"Shade takes refuge at the foot of the trees, as if exhausted along with the travelers."
The dullness of the lotus returns to its root as if languid along with the fish;
the rays of the moon drink up the waters as if scorched by the world;
and sleep enters the inner chamber with beloved women as if exhausted.

In this description of midday, the *sahokti* (concomitance) ornament is employed because of the depiction of the accompaniment of pleasing activities: the shadow takes refuge at the foot of the tree along with travelers; dullness and coolness go to the lower depths of the water along with the fish; the sun’s rays drink the water along with the people; and sleep goes into the inner house along with the women of the harem. However, in such instances as "Sport with him on the shores of the ocean, rustling with palm leaves," there is no *sahokti* ornament because the concomitance lacks aesthetic charm (*acamatkāritva*).
This is the first type of *vinokti* (description by absence).
Vinokti (the figure of speech of "without") occurs when it is stated that the subject at hand is deficient without something else; for example:
"Though knowledge is pleasing, it is blameworthy without the perfection of discipline. (57)

When the subject matter under discussion is described as inferior or base in the absence of something else, it is the figure of speech called *vinokti* (the "without" ornament). For example: "Though learning is pleasing and captivating, it is blameworthy and flawed without the perfection of modesty. Here, the definition is fulfilled because the subject matter under discussion—learning—is stated to be inferior in the absence of the abundance of modesty. *Vinokti* is of two kinds; this is the first type of *vinokti*.
Another example of it is: "He who does not see Rāma, and whom Rāma does not see [is truly lost]."
He will be censured in the world, and even his own self will despise him.

In this case, the inferiority of one who has not obtained the sight of Rāma is shown even without the use of the word "vinā"; thus, it differs from the previous example. The meaning is that without the sight of Rāma, a person becomes censurable.
The second type of *vinokti* is described as follows:
"If something is beautiful without [the absence of] some other thing, that too is called *vinokti*."
O King of kings! This assembly of yours shines resplendent, being entirely free from wicked men. (58)

The word "tat" (that) here refers back to what has been introduced. If that which has been introduced is beautiful or lovely even in the absence of something else, that too is called *vinokti* (the figure of speech of "without"). O King of Kings! "Your assembly shines even without the wicked"—here, because the beauty of the assembly is described in the absence of contact with the wicked, this is the second type of *vinokti*.
Here is another example of it:
Like the night being released from darkness when the moon has appeared,
or like the flame of a nocturnal fire whose smoke has mostly vanished,
this slender-bodied woman is perceived as if almost liberated from her internal delusion.
The Ganges, turbid from falling against its banks, seems to be assuming clarity.

In this case, the loveliness of the night without darkness, of the fire without smoke, of the slender lady without delusion, and of the Gaṅgā without turbidity is made known even without the use of words; thus, it differs from the previous example.
When there is a vivid manifestation of the non-contextual within the contextual, that is *samāsokti* (synecdoche).
O you whose face is like that of Indra’s consort, look! This red moon is kissing [the western horizon]. || 59 ||

When the subject at hand—the description of the relevant event—is being presented, if there occurs a vivid manifestation or cognition of the non-subject—the irrelevant event—due to the similarity of epithets, it is the figure of speech *samāsokti* (abbreviated expression). It is given this etymologically meaningful name because it is an expression (*ukti*) of both the relevant and the irrelevant through abbreviation (*samāsa*). Example: "This moon is red; [the face] of the eastern quarter [is flushed] with wine."

"Look! It kisses—that is, touches—the face, which is the beginning part [of the night]. This is the illustrative example. Here, through the description of the rising moon (*candrodaya*), which is the subject at hand (*prastuta*), there arises the cognition of the unmentioned narrative of a heroine and a hero due to the similarity of qualifiers such as "red" (*rakta*) and so forth; thus, the definition is fully applicable.

For instance, because the word *rakta* (red/passionate) is common to both the literal sense of "red" and the figurative sense of "passionate" through its double meaning (*śleṣa*); because the word *mukha* (mouth/beginning) is common to both "face" and "commencement"; and because the verb *cumbati* (kisses) is common to both "touching with the mouth" and "meeting with the face"—the narrative of a lover attached to another's wife is perceived by means of the masculine gender in the word *candramas* (moon) and the feminine gender in the word *aindrī*, as well as by the connection to Indra implied by those terms. And that perceived meaning embellishes the very subject at hand: the occurrence of the moonrise.

Thus ends the discussion on its nature as an ornament (*alaṅkāra*). The distinction is that in *samāsokti* (speech of brevity), there is the superimposition (*samāropa*) of the behavior (*vyavahāra*) of the non-contextual (*aprastuta*), whereas in *rūpaka* (metaphor), there is the superimposition of the form (*rūpa*) of the non-contextual.
Another example of *samāsokti* is:
"With the burden of her breasts heaving, her hair disheveled, and the strings of her necklace swaying..."

O ball! Since you are cherished with such devotion by this fortunate woman—who sports her cheeks adorned with swinging earrings, whose lotus-face is moist with perspiration, and who, out of passion, incessantly strikes you with her hands while breathing heavily—you are truly blessed.

In this instance, while describing the account of playing with a ball, the account of a heroine engaged in *viparītarata* (reverse sexual union) is understood due to the similarity of the adverbial modifiers such as "with her heavy breasts heaving. The distinction is that in the previous example the adjectives were *śliṣṭa* (punned), whereas here they follow both the primary and secondary subjects even without *śleṣa*. The ornament *parikara* consists of an adjective intended with a specific purpose (*sābhiprāya*). May Śiva, who has the moon as his crest-ornament, remove your distress. (60)

When there is an intentional qualification—that is, when a qualifying attribute is employed with the intention of suggesting a specific meaning that supports the subject matter at hand—the poetic figure named *parikara* (the girdle) occurs. Here, the singular number in the word "viśeṣaṇe" (in the qualification) is not intended to be restrictive. It is designated as the *parikara* ornament because the suggested meaning serves as a "girdle"—that is, an auxiliary or subordinate element—relative to the expressed meaning.

"May Śiva, by whom the moon is worn as an ear-ornament (or crest-ornament) upon his head, remove your distress"—this is an example. Here, the qualifier "by whom the moon is worn as an ornament" is employed with specific intention (*sābhiprāya*), as it serves to establish the sense of removing the distress under discussion. For the capacity of the moon to remove heat is well-established; thus, Śiva, distinguished by that attribute, may remove mental anguish. This constitutes the application of the definition, as the suggested meaning acts as an embellishment (*upaskāraka*) for the contextual subject matter.
Another example of *parikara* follows:
By your grace, even the flower-armed god, having obtained only Madhu as his companion, could cause even Hara, the wielder of the Pināka bow, to lose his fortitude; what then of other archers like me?

Here, the epithet *pinākapāṇeḥ* (the wielder of the Pināka bow) highlights Śiva’s possession of powerful vitality, while the epithet *kusumāyudhaḥ* (he whose weapon is flowers) highlights Manmatha’s possession of a weapon lacking substance. By means of this *kaimutika-nyāya* (argument a fortiori)—suggesting that if I could cause even the wielder of the Pināka to lose his composure, what need is there to mention other archers?—the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*), namely the quality of being the breaker of the composure of all archers, is further embellished; thus, this is the figure of speech *parikara*. However, when the substantive (*viśeṣya*) itself is intended with a specific purpose, it becomes *parikarāṅkura* (the sprout of *parikara*).
For example: "The four-armed God is the bestower of the four aims of human life. (61)

When the substantive (*viśeṣya*) possesses an intended meaning (*sābhiprāya*), and thereby suggests a meaning capable of accomplishing the matter at hand, there is the ornament named *parikarāṅkura* (the sprout of the embellishment). In the verse, "The four-armed Lord Viṣṇu is the giver of the four aims of human life—dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa"—the substantive word "four-armed" (*caturbhuja*) is employed with the intention of implying his capacity to bestow those four aims. This is an example of *parikarāṅkura*. Another example of *parikarāṅkura* is:
"To describe your virtues, O King, the Lord of Serpents [would be required]; to write them down, the Lord of the Haihayas [would be required]."
Who am I to be able to see the entire circle [of your virtues], and what are these qualities of yours?

Here, the meanings—consisting of having a thousand faces, a thousand arms, and a thousand eyes—which are suggested by the words *phaṇīndra* (lord of serpents), *haiyādhipa* (lord of the ocean), and *akhaṇḍala* (Indra) acting as designators (*viśeṣya-vācaka*), are intentional because they serve to establish the capacity for the description of his qualities, the writing [of this work], and the act of seeing. Thus, this is the figure of speech known as *parikara*.

*Śleṣa* (punning) rests upon multiple meanings; it rests upon words (*vāk*), meaning (*artha*), or both. The definition of *śleṣa* is: a deployment of words whose scope consists of multiple meanings. It is of three kinds: 1. *Prakṛta-śleṣa* (contextual punning), which is a deployment of words whose subject matter consists of multiple relevant (*prakṛta*) meanings. 2. *Aprakṛta-śleṣa* (non-contextual punning), which is a deployment of words whose subject matter consists of multiple irrelevant (*aprakṛta*) meanings. 3. *Prakṛtāprakṛta-śleṣa* (mixed punning), which is a deployment of words whose scope consists of multiple relevant and irrelevant meanings. Examples of these are given in order.
An example of *prakṛtaśleṣa* (contextual punning) is as follows:
"May Mādhava, who supported the mountain [Govardhana], protect you—he who is ever-giving (*sarvadā*) and who possesses a cow (*go-mān*). (62)

"He who gives everything" (*sarvadaḥ*) means the giver of all desired objects; "the husband of Māyā" (*māyā-dhavaḥ*) means the husband of Lakṣmī, Viṣṇu, who "bore the mountain" (*adhi-agharaṭ*) Govardhana and the "earth" (*gām*)—may he protect (*pāyāt*). This is one primary meaning. Alternatively, "he who gives everything" (*sarvadā*) refers to Śiva, the husband of Umā, who "bore the *ḍāma*" (*adhīdharat*); may he protect. Since this second meaning is also based on the subject at hand, it is a case of "contextual punning" (*prakṛta-śleṣaḥ*). Another example of this very same [type] is:
"By whom, whose nature is compassion, even the serpent Kākodara was protected..."
May that Lord, renowned for the slaying of Pūtanā, be my refuge.

"May that Rāma, whose very nature is compassion, who protected even the crow—a malicious bird—fearlessly and without dread, be my refuge; and may that Kṛṣṇa, whose name is pure (*pūtanā-mā*), renowned for his slaughter of Pūtanā in battle, and by whom the serpent Kākodara (Kāliya) was protected, be my refuge. Here, because both Rāma and Kṛṣṇa are the subjects under discussion as objects of praise, this is an instance of *prakṛta-śleṣa* (concealment of the contextual). An example of *aprakṛta-śleṣa* (concealment of the non-contextual) is as follows:
"Your face is equal to a lotus (*abja*) that has fixed its attachment upon Hari (Viṣṇu)."

One meaning is: "Your face is equal to the lotus (*abja*)—the lotus (*paṃka-ja*) which has its attachment fixed (*āhita-sakti*) upon the sun (*hariṇa*), that is, the sun (*sūrya*). The second meaning is: "Your face is equal to the moon (*abja*)—the moon (*indu*) which has its attachment fixed (*āhita-sakti*) upon the deer (*hariṇa*), that is, the deer (*mṛga*). Since both the lotus and the moon serve as points of comparison (*upamāna*) and are therefore not the subject under discussion (*aprakṛta*), this is *aprakṛta-śleṣa* (simile-based punning on non-contextual elements).
Here is another example of the same:
"Of those [bees] who have been brought to a state of agitation by many greedy arrows..."
It is like seeing you, who have grown in the forest, among lotuses of similar appearance.

[This verse] is like lotuses (*kamala*) grown and flourishing in water and forest, which have been brought to a state of agitation by many bees—*śilī-murava*s—that are greedy for [the sight of] you and longing for honey; and it is like deer grown in the forest, which have been brought to a state of agitation by hunters (*lubdha*) with *śilī-murava* arrows. Since the words *pada* (lotus) and *hariṇa* (deer) serve as points of comparison (*upamāna*), they are non-contextual; thus, this is an instance of *aprakṛta-śleṣa* (non-contextual paronomasia). According to the *Viśva* lexicon: "The word *kamala* denotes a species of deer.
This is an example of *prakṛtāprakṛta-śleṣa* (paronomasia involving both contextual and non-contextual meanings).
Emitting a torrent of blood, the commander of the army shone resplendently. || 63 ||

The contextual meaning (*prākaraṇikārtha*) is: "The commander of the army (*vāhinīpati*), from whom much *kīlāla*—that is, blood—was gushing forth and rising up, shone resplendently. The non-contextual meaning (*aprākaraṇikārtha*) is: "The lord of rivers (*vāhinīpati*)—the ocean—from which much *kīlāla*—that is, water—was gushing forth, shone resplendently. Because this *śleṣa* (punning conjunction) pertains to both the contextual and the non-contextual meanings, it is a *prakṛtāprakṛta-śleṣa* (conjunction of the contextual and non-contextual). (In this case, a similarity between the contextual and non-contextual subjects is perceived.
Here is another example of this very same [type]:
"He has ascended the mountain peak (*udaya*), he is radiant, and his orb (*maṇḍala*) is red..."
The king captivates the hearts of the world with his gentle rays.

In this context, the contextual meaning (*prākaraṇikārtha*) is as follows: the king, a sovereign who has attained rise and prosperity, whose orb is red, and whose subjects are devoted to him, wins over and captivates the hearts of the people with soft taxes—that is, wealth to be taken [gently]. The non-contextual meaning (*aprākaraṇikārtha*) is: the moon, a king who has ascended the mountain of sunrise, whose orb is reddish, wins over the hearts of the people with its gentle rays. Because words that are shared (*śliṣṭapada*) have as their scope both the contextual and the non-contextual meanings, this is "conjoined metaphor" (*prakṛtāprakṛta-śleṣa*).

The following point should be noted here: in instances such as "sarvado mādhavaḥ" (Mādhava gives everything), "yo’gaṅgām" (he who [crossed] the Gaṅgā), and "īśi hitasaktinā" (by one whose devotion is fixed on the Lord), there is *sabhaṅgaśleṣa* (pun with word-splitting), because multiple meanings are conveyed in dependence upon mutually distinct word-divisions (*padabhaṅga*). In cases such as "abjakīlālavāhinīpati," multiple meanings are conveyed without depending on any division of the words themselves; thus, there is *abhaṅgaśleṣa* (pun without word-splitting). In this manner, *atiśleṣa* (superlative pun) is twofold.

Regarding *śleṣa* (paronomasia) involving both the relevant (*prakṛta*) and the irrelevant (*aprakṛta*), some hold the view that the irrelevant meaning is suggested (*vyaṅgya*). Others, however, while accepting that this [irrelevant meaning] is also directly expressed (*vācya*), maintain that the non-difference or the similarity between the relevant and the irrelevant is what is suggested. In the first view, an example of *śleṣa* involving both the relevant and the irrelevant should not be cited; in the second view, an example of *vastudhvani* based on the power of words (*śabdaśaktimūla*) should not be cited. *Aprastutapraśaṃsā* (Indirect Description) occurs where there is a reference to the irrelevant based upon the relevant:
"One among birds is truly successful—he who does not beg from anyone other than Indra. (64)

*Aprastutapraśaṃsā* (Indirect Description) is that description of something not under discussion (*aprastuta*) which, while resting upon what is under discussion (*prastuta*), results ultimately in the comprehension of the matter related to that which is under discussion. The essential definition is: where the matter of something not under discussion is described for the purpose of comprehending the matter of that which is under discussion, there exists *aprastutapraśaṃsā*. An example is: "Among the birds (*śakunta*), he alone is truly successful (*kṛtī*) who does not beg from anyone other than Śakra [Indra]."

In this context, the description of the story of the cātaka bird—similar to the one being presented—is intended to convey the matter at hand: the account of one possessed of such self-respect as to think, "I do not pray to any lord other than the sovereign of the whole earth. Thus, there is a formal consistency with the definition [of the figure of speech].

The comprehension of the relevant (the *prastuta*) through the irrelevant (the *aprastuta*) occurs when there is a relationship between the relevant and the irrelevant. This relationship may be based on similarity (*sārūpya*), the relation of general and particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣabhāva*), or the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). The verse beginning with "One man is successful" (*ekaḥ kṛtī*) is an example of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* based on similarity. Regarding the relation of general and particular, there are two varieties: the comprehension of the particular from the general, or the comprehension of the general from the particular.

Thus, even regarding the relation of cause and effect, there is a twofold understanding: either the cause from the effect, or the effect from the cause. The illustrations for these four cases are to be found in the Appendix. The distinction between these two figures is as follows: in *samāsokti* (brief expression), the understanding of the non-contextual event arises from the contextual one through the power of double-entendre (*śliṣṭa*) adjectives; whereas in *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect description), the comprehension of the contextual arises from the non-contextual by means of a relationship such as similarity (*sārūpya*). Here is another example of *aprastutapraśaṃsā*:
If a dog, its shoulder-blade made bristly with bound-on artificial manes, were elevated to the rank of the lord of beasts,
it would still be far from the lion who is ever eager to split the temples of rutting elephants.

"How will the dog, though placed upon the track of the lord of beasts, roar like the lord of deer? Here, the description of the irrelevant account of the dog—which concludes by applying to the conduct of a fool who, through mere artificial dress and behavior, attempts to act like a wise man due to a superficial resemblance—constitutes *Aprastutapraśaṃsā* (Indirect Praise).
When the relevant is illuminated by the relevant, it is *Prastutāṅkura* (The Sprout of the Relevant).
O bee, what is the use of the thorny *ketakī* when the *mālatī* is present?

The ornament named *prastutāṅkura* (the sprout of the relevant) occurs when, by means of describing one relevant subject, another relevant subject that is intended is illuminated. An example is: "O bee, while the *mālatī* is present, what is the use of the *ketakī*, which is filled with thorns? Here, for a woman sporting in a garden with her beloved, there is the *prastutāṅkura* ornament because of the mention of association with another woman who possesses many defects.

In the speech of a noble lady who desires to turn her lover away, both the literal meaning (*vācyārtha*)—the bee’s gathering [of nectar]—and the contextual meaning—her reproach that he is attached to other women—are equally relevant to the context; thus, the definition is fully satisfied.
Here is another example of *prastutāṅkura* (the sprout of the relevant): "O bee, first toward those other flowers which are capable of withstanding pressure..."
Divert your restless mind toward the flowering creepers;
why do you pointlessly torment the young jasmine bud, which has not yet reached its season, out of time?

Here too, since both the expressed meaning—the reproach of the bee—and the suggested meaning—the reproach of the lover who, despite the presence of mature women, torments a young girl for the sake of pleasure—are relevant to the context, this is the figure of speech *prastutāṅkura* (the sprout of the relevant). In these two examples, because the expressed meaning is relevant, the primary function of denotation (*abhidhā*) rests there; yet, through the power of the beauty of the meaning, the intended meaning is perceived as *dhvani* (suggestion) itself, not as a mere figure of speech.

Some maintain that the status of being an *alaṅkāra* (poetic figure) belongs only to that where the suggested meaning serves as an embellishment for the expressed meaning. According to their view, the following is an example of the *prastutāṅkura* (the sprout of the relevant) *alaṅkāra*, which will be discussed hereafter:
"This lotus plant bears a pair of buds pierced by the beaks of *kādamba* geese;
the mango creeper holds a fresh sprout tasted by the male cuckoo."

Having heard these words of her friends spoken among themselves, she concealed the slope of her breasts with the hem of her garment on the bank of the pond, and covered her bimba-like lips with her hand.

"This lotus-pond bears a pair of buds pecked by the beaks of swans; likewise, this mango-creeper bears a fresh sprout tasted by the cuckoo"—having heard this conversation among her companions on the bank of the pond, the heroine who had just arrived understood that they were describing the state of her own breasts and lips under the pretext of the lotus buds and mango shoots. Realizing this, she concealed the slope of her breast with the hem of her garment and her lower lip with her hand; herein lies the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*) of another contextual subject.

Because the poet himself has revealed it in the second half of the verse, it constitutes an *alaṅkāra* (poetic figure). Thus it is said in the *Dhvanyāloka*: "Where a suggested meaning, which was already implied by the power of the word and its sense, is further revealed by the poet through his own explicit statement—that is another variety of *dhvani* known as *alaṅkāra*."
First, *paryāyokta* (periphrasis):
*Paryāyokta*, however, is the expression of what is implied by resorting to a different mode of speech.
"Salutation to Him by whom the breasts of Rāhu’s wife were rendered useless [in their effort to hide]! (66)

*Paryāyokta* (periphrasis) is the expression of a meaning intended to be conveyed by resorting to a different mode of speech—that is, its description through a manner more charming than the one actually intended. This is based on the etymological derivation: *paryāyeṇa* (by way of a different mode) *uktam* (spoken), where that which was intended (*vivakṣitam*) is expressed (*abhihitam*) by means of a different turn of phrase. An example is: "Salutation to that Vāsudeva, by whom the breasts of Rāhu’s wife were rendered futile and useless," because he reduced Rāhu to a mere headless trunk.

Here, because the Blessed One—who is to be understood through His own unique form as Vāsudeva—is described by means of a different mode (bhaṅgyantara) as being the cause of the futility of Rāhu’s wife’s breasts, there is a correspondence with the definition of *paryāyokta* (periphrasis).
Another example of this very same [figure] is as follows:
"He whose foot beholds the world does not behold his own foot."
Even by those two, the knowledge of you, the teacher of the universe, cannot be fully discerned.

The foot of Akṣapāda, by whom the world is seen, is that very world which does not see the foot of Patañjali (the incarnation of Ādiśeṣa). Your knowledge, O Teacher of the Universe, is immeasurable compared to those two—Gautama and Patañjali—who are here indicated by their own unique forms as Akṣapāda and Patañjali, yet expressed through other forms. This is *paryāyokta* (periphrasis). They also say that the second type of *paryāyokta* is that which achieves a desired end through a pretext.
"I am going to see the mango creeper; you two should sit here."

They say that *paryāyokta* (periphrasis) is also the accomplishment of one's own desired object or another's desired task by means of a pretext—that is, under the guise of some other business. The essential point is that the second type of *paryāyokta* consists in the accomplishment of a desired task through the pretext of another task. An example is: "I am going—I shall go—to see the mango-creeper; you two should remain—stay right here."

In this instance, a female friend, desiring to provide a secluded place for the heroine and hero—who are feeling bashful in her presence—for their amorous play, accomplishes her own desired aim or that which is desired by the couple under the pretext of pointing out a mango creeper; thus, the definition of the second type of *paryāyokta* (periphrasis) is fully applicable.
Another example of this is:
"O Rādhā, give me back my ball, hidden beneath your garment."
Thus loosening her waist-knot—may that Kṛṣṇa be for our delight.

In this case, by means of the pretext of loosening her waist-knot (*nīvī*) for the purpose of cleaning the ball (*kanduka*), Kṛṣṇa accomplishes his own desired end; thus, there is a second type of *paryāyokta* (periphrasis).
"Speech" (*ukti*) consists of praise or censure expressed through the guise of censure or praise.

The *vyājastuti* (feigned praise) ornament consists in the expression or manifestation of praise through censure, or of censure through praise. The essential definition is that *vyājastuti* occurs when praise is understood under the guise of censure, or censure is understood under the guise of praise. Thus, *vyājastuti* is of two kinds: praise by means of censure, and censure by means of praise. It should be understood that the etymological derivation of the term *nindā-vyāja-stuti* follows this sequence: praise under the guise of censure (*nindā-vyāja-stuti*), and censure in the form of a feigned praise (*vyāja-stuti*).
An example of *vyājastuti* consisting in the understanding of praise through censure is as follows: [Example omitted per instructions]
O Svardhunī, what discernment is yours that you lead sinners to heaven?

"O Gaṅgā, who flows through the heavens, what discernment do you possess? You have no discernment," [it is said] because you lead even sinners to heaven; here, under the guise of censure—that you lack discernment—there is actually a praise for the excellence of Gaṅgā’s power, namely her capacity to grant heaven by pacifying the sins even of great offenders. This is *vyājastuti* (disguised praise).
Another example of this is:
"What pride of valor do you have to boast of in battle when you are mounted upon but a single horse?"
Mounted upon the seven-horsed chariot, they become adversaries.

In this case, when the king has mounted a single horse to fight, his enemies become mounted upon seven horses; therefore, under the guise of censuring the king’s pride in his valor—saying "let there be no such arrogance"—the king is actually praised for his heroism by the fact that he was killed in battle and went to heaven after piercing the solar orb. This is *vyājastuti* (ironical praise), which consists of praise through the medium of censure. The term "seven horses" (*sapta-saptayaḥ*) refers to the Sun; thus, the construction can be understood in two ways: either as "the Sun who possesses seven horses," or as "those seven who are the horses. This is an example of *vyājastuti* where censure is understood through the medium of praise.
"Excellent, messenger! Excellent indeed! What more could be done than this, that for my sake you have been torn apart even by teeth and by nails? (69)

"O messenger, well done! Well done again! (Since you have performed something worthy of praise, you are) indeed praiseworthy. What more remains to be done? For you have been torn and mangled with nails and teeth for my sake. Here, a heroine—who has learned the truth by observing the tooth and nail marks visible on her own body because the messenger, having been sent to bring the hero, had herself experienced sexual union with him—thus censures her under the guise of praise. Therefore, this is *vyājastuti* (ironical praise), wherein praise culminates in censure.
Another example of this is:
"O Lord, half of Śiva was taken by the enemy of the Dānavas, and half by the Daughter of the Mountain; thus, on the surface of the earth, the absence of the Destroyer of Smara manifests."
The Ganges, the ocean, the sky, the crescent moon, the lord of serpents, Matali, omniscience, and sovereignty have come to you; while for me, there is only the wandering for alms.

In this verse, the petitioner praises the king as if saying, "The omniscience and supreme lordship of Lord Śiva were taken away from him by Hari and Pārvatī, but the act of wandering for alms fell upon me"; yet, by doing so, he actually censures the king: "Though you are all-knowing and the lord of all, having recognized both my scholarship and my poverty, you give me nothing. This is *vyājastuti* (disguised praise). When censure is expressed through the medium of censure, it is called *vyājanindā* (disguised censure):
"O Creator! He alone is to be censured who formerly cut off only one head! (70)

The manifestation or disclosure of one censure through the censure of another is the poetic figure known as *vyājanindā* (disguised censure). An example is: "O Creator, O Brahmā, that Hara who formerly severed [only] a single head is himself censurable. Here, by means of the censure of Hara, the intended censure of Brahmā—who set in motion this worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) with its terrible consequences—is understood; thus, it is the figure of *vyājanindā*.
Another example of indirect censure (vyājanindā):
"O crow, you alone are particularly deserving of reproach;
what fault is yours that you cause the sweet-voiced cuckoo to dwell with the mango tree?"

Here, by censuring the ritual injunction, the crow is being condemned for its harsh, ear-piercing cawing; this is "disguised censure" (vyājanindā). First is "objection" (ākṣepa): "Objection is the denial of what has been stated by oneself, following from deliberation."
O Moon, reveal yourself, or else show the face of my beloved.

The poetic figure named *ākṣepa* (paralipsis) is a negation of a matter already stated by oneself, undertaken with some underlying motive. An example is: "O Moon, show yourself, or else [show] the face of my beloved. Here, the sight of the moon is first requested;

subsequently, considering the sight of the moon to be purposeless because the face of the beloved—which is inherently delightful—is present, the indication of a negation through the alternative "or else" (*athavā*) establishes the application of the definition of the *ākṣepa* figure.
Another example of the first type of *ākṣepa* follows.
O lords of poets, preserve this nectar for the ears produced from churning the ocean of literature,
for the thieves of poetic meaning are ready to plunder it like Daityas.

Let everyone take [these works] as they wish; there is no harm whatsoever for the lords of poets. Even when many jewels have been taken away by the immortals, the ocean remains a mine of gems even today.

Here, with the first verse, the protection of the poem from those who would steal its meaning is requested. Subsequently, by considering the inexhaustibility of the wonders of the poet’s expression and stating "let everyone take [what they wish]," a prohibition against such appropriation is established; this constitutes the *ākṣepa* (paradoxical objection).
Some scholars consider this second *ākṣepa* to be an *ākṣepa* that appears as a prohibition (*niṣedhābhāsa*).
I am not her messenger; the torment of her body is like the fire of cosmic destruction.

Some scholars consider *ākṣepa* (paralipsis) to be a semblance of negation (*niṣedhābhāsa*) that takes the form of a negation. Thus, the definition of the second type of *ākṣepa* is: "Paralipsis is a semblance of negation. An example is: "I am not a messenger; the heat of her body—the bodily torment—is like the fire of cosmic destruction (*kālānala*), equal to the fire at the time of universal dissolution" (meaning it is utterly unbearable). This is the speech of a messenger sent by a heroine who is tormented by the pain of unbearable separation, addressed to the hero.

The prohibition "I am not a messenger" (*nāhaṃ dūtī*), being contradicted here, takes on the form of its opposite; it culminates in the sense: "I am not one who speaks deceitful words appropriate for a conciliation, but I speak only the truth. By implying the specific detail that the heroine must be brought back to life this very moment, there is the figure of speech *Ākṣepa* (Paralipsis). Another example of the second type of *Ākṣepa* is: "O crest-jewel of kings, we are not carriers of royal messages."
To you, who are the father of the universe, no enemy whatsoever is seen today.

Here, in the speech of the messengers, the denial "we are not carriers of a message" is sublated; having thus become a semblance of that [denial], it culminates in truthful speaking by avoiding the deceitful words appropriate for a conversation during a truce. This implies the specific point: "all kings—even enemies—must be protected like one's own family. This is the third type of *ākṣepa* (paraleipsis): "Another *ākṣepa* occurs when an injunction is manifested and a negation is concealed."
Go, O beloved! If you must go, may my birth be right there with you. (73)

When an injunction (*vidhi*) is manifest and clear, while a prohibition (*niṣedha*) is concealed and indistinct, there occurs a third type of *ākṣepa* (paralipsis). The essential definition is that where an undesired injunction is made explicit and clear, while the desired prohibition is revealed through a different turn of phrase in an indistinct manner, that is *ākṣepa*. An example is: "O beloved, if you go, then go; if you must certainly depart, then let it be so. Wherever you go, there alone shall be my birth."

In this instance, although the beloved’s departure to a distant land is undesirable, the permission for him to go—expressed as "Go"—is clearly manifested. Furthermore, by the indirect suggestion (bhaṅgyantareṇa) that "may my rebirth occur right there," it is indicated that in separation her own death will surely follow; thus, the prohibition of the departure is revealed through concealment. This constitutes the application of the definition [of *ākṣepa*]. Another example of the third type of *ākṣepa* is:
"Your journey will not cause me long-lasting distress."
If you must go, then go; enough with even this suspicion of yours.
In this case, by indicating his own death, the prohibition against the journey is implied.
When there is an appearance of contradiction despite the absence of actual contradiction, it is considered a "semblance of contradiction" (virodhābhāsa).
"O slender one, even without a necklace, your breasts are captivating. (74)

When a contradiction appears to manifest at first sight but is resolved in the final conclusion, it is accepted as the poetic figure known as *virodhābhāsa* (semblance of contradiction). O slender one, the contradiction manifests that "your breasts (*vakṣojau*) are captivating (*hāriṇau*) even without a necklace (*hāra*"); then, by resolving this contradiction through interpreting the word *hāriṇau* to mean "captivating the mind" (*manohāriṇau*), there occurs the *virodhābhāsa*.
Another example of *virodhābhāsa* is:

"What fear can there be from those [enemies], who, like rival kings (*pratīpabhūpaiḥ*), have abandoned their capacity to divide [the world] despite possessing contradictory qualities (*viruddhadharmaiḥ*)?"
That conqueror of enemies and conqueror of friends by his prowess moved about with discerning vision, even while observing through his spies.

Here, although there appears to be a contradiction at first glance in the statement "Nala, though a conqueror of enemies (*amitrajit*), is by his splendor a conqueror of friends (*mitrajit*); though his gaze is directed toward discernment (*vicāradṛg*), he has the gaze of a spy (*cāradṛk*),"—the resolution of this contradiction is as follows: he is indeed a conqueror of enemies (*amitrāṇām*, i.e., foes), yet by his splendor (*ojasā*) he is a conqueror of the Sun (*mitrasya*, the friend); likewise, he is one who has fixed his sight on discernment (*vicāre*), yet he possesses the vision of a spy (*cāra*). Thus, it is a "semblance of contradiction" (*virodhābhāsa*). First, regarding *vibhāvanā*:
"There may be *vibhāvanā* even without a cause, if the production of an effect occurs."
"Even though not sprinkled with lac-dye, your two feet are red.

(75) The figure of speech *vibhāvanā* occurs when an effect is described as arising even in the absence of its well-known cause—that is, even without a cause. It is called *vibhāvanā* because another [implied] cause is "discerned" (*vibhāvyate*) therein. O beloved, your two feet have become red—meaning crimson—even without being sprinkled with lac-dye; that is, even without the application of lac-dye. Since the redness of the feet is here described as arising despite the absence of the well-known cause, which is the application of lac-dye, this is the figure of speech *vibhāvanā*.
The resolution of the contradiction arises from the fact that redness is natural [to the lotus].

There are six types of *vibhāvanā* (poetic conceit): the production of an effect in the absence of its cause; the production of an effect despite the deficiency of its causes; the production of an effect despite the presence of an obstacle; the production of an effect from what is not its cause; the production of an effect contrary [to expectation]; and the production of a cause from its effect. This is another example of the first type of *vibhāvanā*.
The world was enchanting: its kādamba birds were not yet drunk from drinking, its stainless sky was not yet swept clear, and its subtle waters had not yet become limpid.

Here, although the well-known causes—drinking, cleansing, and clearing—are absent, there is a description of the arising of effects in the form of intoxication, stainlessness, and subtlety; thus, it is *vibhāvanā* (the description of an effect in the absence of its cause). The contradiction is resolved by attributing [these effects] to the season of autumn as their cause.
Furthermore, the second type of *vibhāvanā* is considered to be the arising of an effect when the causes are incomplete.
With weapons that are neither sharp nor hard, Manmatha conquers the world.

The second *vibhāvanā* (the description of the production of an effect despite the incompleteness or deficiency of causes) occurs when one describes the arising of an effect even though the causes are not complete. In the case of "Manmatha conquers the world with weapons that are neither sharp nor hard," there is *vibhāvanā* because one describes the production of the effect—the conquest of the world—even while the causes, the weapons, lack qualities such as sharpness.
Another example of this very same [figure] is:
"The pollen of mango and campaka flowers, stirred up by the garden breeze..."
They cause travelers to weep, yet they do not touch their eyes.
Here, even though the action of touching is absent, there is *vibhāvanā* because the effect— the rising of tears— is produced by the dust.
This would be the third *vibhāvanā*, wherein the production of an effect occurs despite the presence of an obstacle.
O King! That serpent-like sword bites only the lords of men. ||77||

If the production of an effect is described despite the presence of an obstacle, that is the third *vibhāvanā*. O King, in the case where it is said, "Your sword alone—a serpent indeed—bites the lords of men—who are themselves physicians of poison," there is the description of the production of an effect (the biting) even though obstacles to a snake's bite, such as mantras and medicinal herbs, are present; thus, this is the third *vibhāvanā*. The resolution of the contradiction occurs through the pun (*śleṣa*) on the word *narendra*, which here signifies "king.
Another example of this is: "The breeze comes from the *tila* flower, cool as sandalwood."
