Bees emerge from the variegated pair of blue lotuses.

Here, there is a *vibhāvanā* based on the production [of something] from a cause that is different [from what is expected], namely, the wind cooled by sandalwood arising from a sesame flower. The resolution of the apparent contradiction (*virodha*) occurs through the identification (*abhedādhyavasāna*) of the sesame flower with the heroine’s nose, and of the wind with her breath.
A certain type of *vibhāvanā* is observed where the accomplishment of an effect arises from a contrary cause; this is the fifth *vibhāvanā*.
Alas, the rays of the cool-rayed moon cause distress to that slender woman.

The fifth type of *vibhāvanā* (poetic figure of "extraordinary causation") is the production of an effect from a contradictory cause—that is, the arising of an effect from a cause that is diametrically opposed to it. In the verse, "The rays of the cool-rayed moon [usually] cause distress to the slender maiden," the moonbeams—which by their very nature of coolness should remove heat—instead produce heat in the slender maiden; thus, this is the fifth *vibhāvanā*, consisting of the production of an effect from a contradictory cause. The resolution of the contradiction lies in the fact that the slender maiden is a woman separated from her lover (*virahiṇī*). Another example of this is:
"When the young sun has risen, the blue water-lily blooms, but the constellation does not shine."
The variegated lotus-hands of the princes of rival kings close like buds.

In this case, when the sun has risen, the blue lily (*kuvalaya*) blossoms, the stars shine, and the lotuses close; thus, the production of an effect from a contrary cause is described. By interpreting it as: "The prince alone is the sun; when he rises, the circle of the earth (*bhūmaṇḍala*) shines, the warrior class (*kṣatra*) does not gleam, and the hands of the enemy princes—which are themselves lotuses—close up," the contradiction is resolved.
A sixth type of *vibhāvanā* is also observed: that in which an effect is seen to arise even from a non-cause.
The mass of your fame was borne by the hand that was like a wish-fulfilling tree.

*Ṣaṣṭhī Vibhāvanā* (the sixth type of *vibhāvanā*) occurs when, transgressing the rule that "the effect arises from the cause," one describes the arising of the cause from the effect. For example, in the verse: "Your hand alone is the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpataru*); from it [arises] fame, which is an ocean of milk. Here, by describing the arising of the wish-fulfilling tree from the ocean of milk—thereby transgressing the well-known relationship of cause and effect where the ocean is the cause and the tree the effect—the figure is *vibhāvanā*. The resolution of the apparent contradiction (*virodha*) is that fame arises from the hand of a king who is habitually generous. Another example of this follows.
Indeed, a creeper is born upon a mountain, but a mountain is never born from a creeper;
now, however, the opposite has occurred, for two mountains have been born upon a golden creeper.

In this case, the production of a cause from an effect is described by stating that "two mountains were born upon Kanakalatā. The resolution of the contradiction is achieved through the intended meaning (*vivakṣā*), where the word "Kanakalatā" refers to the body of a passionate woman and the phrase "two mountains" refers to her pair of breasts.
The figure of speech called *viśeṣokti* (peculiar statement) is the non-production of an effect despite the presence of a complete set of causes, as in:
"Even while the lamp of love was burning, the waning of affection did not occur in the heart of the husband."

When a complete cause—that is, a full set of causal factors—is present, yet the effect does not arise, this is the figure of speech named *viśeṣokti* (peculiar causation). In the verse "Even while the lamp of love burns in the heart, there is no depletion of oil," there is no depletion of oil—meaning no depletion of affection—even though the burning of the lamp is present, which is the cause for such depletion; thus, because the non-depletion is described despite the presence of its cause, it is *viśeṣokti*. The resolution of the apparent contradiction (*virodha*) lies in the intended meaning that, although love is blazing, there is no loss of affection. The distinction between these two figures is as follows: *vibhāvanā* is the arising of an effect in the absence of its cause, whereas *viśeṣokti* is the non-arising of an effect when its cause is present.
Another example of the statement of distinction (viśeṣokti) is:
"The twilight is full of passion, and the day precedes it;
oh, how strange is the course of fate, yet even so, there is no union."

Here, although the cause for their meeting exists, the description of its non-occurrence constitutes *viśeṣokti* (the figure of particularity). And the reason for this is stated: "Oh, how strange is the course of fate!
*Asambhava* (the impossible) is the description of the impossibility of accomplishing an object, as in:
"Who knows if a cowherd boy could uproot a mountain?"

The description of the impossibility of the accomplishment of a purpose—that is, the success of an action—is the figure of speech *asaṃbhava* (impossibility). "Who knows (*ko veda*), who indeed perceived, that Kṛṣṇa, though but a child (*apaśiśuka*), might uproot (*utpāṭayet*) Mount Govardhana?"—here, because the uprooting of the mountain by a child is described as impossible, it is the figure of *asaṃbhava*.
Another example of impossibility is:
"He alone is the abode of waters; he is the mine of jewels (*ratnākara*)."
We, whose minds were agitated by thirst, have resorted to this ocean;
who could have known that the Sage would drink it up— along with its gasping whales and sea-monsters— by means of the hollow of his own cupped palms?

"Who could have known that the sage Agastya would drink up the ocean, the reservoir of waters, in this manner! By thus describing the impossibility of the sage drinking the ocean, there is the figure of speech *asaṃbhava* (the impossible).
First is *asaṅgati* (incongruity):
"Incongruity is the contradiction of cause and effect through their being located in different places."
The clouds have drunk the poison; the wives of travelers have fainted.

The figure of speech *asaṃgati* (inconsistency) occurs when there is a description of spatial separation (*bhinnadeśatva*) between two cause and effect (*kārya-hetu*) that is contradictory—that is, their existence in different locations is logically untenable. The underlying sense is that *asaṃgati* does not apply in cases where such spatial separation between cause and effect is not contradictory.

The clouds (*jalaghara*) have drunk the poison (*viṣa*, i.e., water), and the wives of travelers (*pathikāṅganā*), who are separated from their husbands, have fainted; here, because the drinking of poison is attributed to the clouds and the resulting fainting to the wives of travelers, there is a formal application (*samanvaya*) of the definition of *asaṅgati* (incongruity) based on describing cause and effect as being in contradictory and different locations. The resolution of this contradiction lies in the fact that the clouds, having drunk water, act as excitants of passion, whereby the wives of travelers faint. *Asaṅgati* is of three kinds.

[Inconsistency] consists of the effect and the cause being located in different places; performing elsewhere what ought to be done in one place; and performing the opposite of what one intends to do. Among these, the following is an example of the first type of inconsistency:
"Oh, how strange is this method of killing employed by the serpent-like rogue! This is another example of it.
One person bites the ear of another, and that other is deprived of his life-breaths.

In this case, a wicked serpent bites the ear of one person, while another is deprived of life; thus, there is *asaṅgati* (incongruity) due to the description of the cause and its effect being in different locations. The resolution of the contradiction (*virodhaparihāra*) is that Bala tells something into the ear of someone, and by that, the death of another occurs.
The second type of *asaṅgati* is:
"It is that which consists of performing elsewhere what ought to be performed in a place other than that."
Desiring to rid the earth of the pārijāta tree, you acted in such a way toward heaven.

What is *asaṅgati*? It is the performance (*kṛti*) of an action intended for one place in another location—that is, in a different substratum. (O Kṛṣṇa! Desiring to make the earth (*vasudhā*) devoid of the *Ari-jāta* (the multitude of enemies), you likewise made heaven (*dyauḥ*) devoid of the *Pārijāta* (the celestial tree). Here, because the state of being "devoid of the *Ari-jāta*"—which was to be accomplished on the earth—is described as being accomplished in heaven, the definition of *asaṅgati* is fully applicable.

In the verse beginning with "apārijātām," the incongruity that appears through the identification based on punning (śleṣamūlakābhedādhyavasāna) is resolved by providing separate applications of meaning for both the side of the earthly king and the side of heaven.
Another example of this is: "tvatsaṅgakhaṇḍitasapatnavilāsinīnām... [and so forth].

O sole hero of the world, O lion among the lords of Cola, fresh ornaments appear upon you: bracelets upon your eyes, leaf-patterned vines upon your thighs, and a tilaka-mark upon your sprout-like hands.

In this case, the wives of those enemies slain by Colendra place bracelets on their eyes, leaf-patterns on their thighs, and forehead-marks on their sprout-like hands. This constitutes the figure *asaṅgati* (incongruity), because ornaments that ought to be applied elsewhere—such as on the arms, breasts, and foreheads—are instead described as being applied to other parts, such as the eyes and so forth. The resolution of this apparent contradiction (*virodhaparihāra*) is that such a state is observed among the weeping women who have placed the [enemy's] head, struck off, upon their own heads. The third type of *asaṅgati* is defined as the performance of an action contrary to that which one had set out to do.
Although you were intent on upholding the lineage, you brought about its dissolution in the past. || 85 ||

The third type of incongruity (*asaṅgati*) consists in the performance of an action contrary to that which one has set out to do—namely, the performance of an act opposed to the intended task. (O Kṛṣṇa! Although you previously set out to "uplift the earth" (*gotroddhāra*)—that is, to raise her from the depths during your Varāha incarnation—you instead performed the "shattering of the mountains" (*gotrodbheda*), meaning the breaking apart of the peaks (*gotra* = *parvata*) by means of the striking of your hooves and so forth. Here, because there is a description of performing the shattering of the mountains—which is contrary to the upliftment of the earth—for one who had set out for that very upliftment, there is incongruity.
The contradiction is resolved through punning (*śleṣa*).
Another example of this follows.
O Lord of all, having assumed this form for the sake of removing the delusion of embodied beings throughout the three worlds, you have,
by means of this very [form], [acted] with an ocean of the nectar of boundless splendor.
You increase the delusion of those charmingly playful women.

In this case, the incongruity (*asaṅgati*) consists in the Lord, having assumed a form intended to remove delusion, instead increasing the delusion of those with charming eyes—an action contrary to his initial purpose. The resolution of this contradiction is that by assuming a form to turn back the ignorance of people, he increases the passion of those with charming eyes.
First, the *viṣama* (the incongruous) is described as that in which two things are depicted as incompatible with one another:
"Where is this girl with limbs as soft as the *śirīṣa* flower, and where is the god whose banner is the sea-monster? (86)

The figure of speech *viṣama* (the incongruous) occurs where the conjunction—that is, the connection—of two things that are incompatible and dissimilar is described. In the verse, "Where is this woman, whose limbs are as soft as the *śirīṣa* flower, and where is such a god of love? there is the figure *viṣama* because of the conjunction of the woman and the god of love, who are dissimilar by virtue of being exceedingly delicate and exceedingly unbearable, respectively. This *viṣama* is of three kinds: consisting of the conjunction of unlike things, consisting of the production of an effect contrary [to expectations], and consisting of the attainment of an undesired result despite striving for a desired object. Of these, the following is an example of the first kind.

O Moon, if you wish to describe another example of the first type of unevenness (*viṣama*), then plunge once more into the ocean and wash away the mark upon your face, which is the beauty of the deer-eyed woman’s countenance! Alas!
Therefore, perfume this exceedingly pure reflection with the blossoms of the Pārijāta tree; tell me, otherwise, where is her face and where is this?

Here, because of the union of two dissimilar things—the moon-like face and the mark—there is the "uneven" (viṣama). A second type of the uneven is considered another form of the uneven: the production of an effect that is contrary [to its cause].
Your dark little sword produces white fame.

The second type of *viṣama* (the incongruous) consists in the description of the production of a quality in the effect that is contrary to the quality of the cause. The application of the definition is seen here because of the description of the production of white fame—which is contrary to it—from a dark-colored dagger. When the effect possesses qualities distinct from those of the cause, it is the figure of speech *viṣama*; whereas when the cause brings about an effect contrary to its own nature, it is the fifth type of *vibhāvanā* (poetic fancy)—such is the distinction between these two. The third type of *viṣama* is: "The attainment of even the undesirable resulting from an effort toward a desired object."
A mouse, seeing a chest of snakes with the hope of eating them, was bitten by one and devoured by it. || 88 ||

From the exertion for a desired object—that is, from the effort toward a wished-for goal—not only is the desired object not obtained, but even the attainment of the undesired occurs; that is the third type of *viṣama* (the incongruous).

A mouse (*ākhu*), out of a desire for food—the thirst for obtaining edible things—having seen a snake-casket (*ahimañjūṣā*) and having gnawed through it, was eaten by that very snake. In this case, for the mouse who exerted itself for the sake of food, not only was the food not obtained, but there was also the attainment of the undesired, namely death; thus, this is the third *viṣama*. Here is another example of the third *viṣama*:
O Kṛṣṇa, thinking "I am a cowherd," you resorted to the desire for abundant milk;
yet even the milk from your mother's breast was rendered unobtainable by you.

In this case, the non-attainment of the desired—namely, abundant milk—and the attainment of the undesired—namely, the failure to obtain the mother’s breast milk—constitute the third type of *viṣama* (the incongruous).
First, regarding *sama* (the concordant):
*Sama* is that description wherein two things that are mutually appropriate [are presented as such].
The circle of her breasts was made to match [her] by the necklace. 89.

As the counterpart to the figure of speech *viṣama* (the Uneven), *sama* (the Even) is also threefold: consisting of the description of two similar things, consisting of the arising of a similar effect, and consisting of the attainment of the desired without the undesired. Where the relationship between two similar things is described, there is the first type of *sama*. In the example, "By means of her necklace, her circle of breasts has been made its own worthy abode," the figure is *samālaṅkāra* because of the description of the relationship between the two similar things—the necklace and the circle of breasts.
This is another illustration of the first type of *sama*.

O King Narasiṃha, behold how your fame shines, having taken refuge in you who are its worthy match— just as the moonlight rests upon the orb of the cool-rayed moon, or as the Ganges upon the ornament of the crescent moon.
Here, because of the fitting conjunction of the Kaumudī moon-maṇḍala, the Jāhnavī-like moon-crested Lord, and the kings of fame, there is the figure of speech *samālaṅkāra*.
They know a second type of *sama* as that where even the effect possesses similarity with its cause.
O Lakṣmī, born from the lotus, your inclination toward the lowly is indeed fitting for you.

The second type of *sama* (similarity) is known by the learned as the similarity of the effect with its cause, consisting in the possession of common qualities. O Lakṣmī, for you who were born from water, a tendency toward the lowly—that is, a disposition to follow the base—is appropriate; here, because the quality of the cause, namely the water’s tendency toward the lowly, is described in the effect, Lakṣmī, it is the figure of speech *sama*. "Lowly" (*nīca*) refers both to a low place and to a base person.
Another example of the second *sama* is: "The smoke produced from a forest fire, having attained density, [is extinguished] by rains."
That which he pacifies is joined with him, for he too indeed consumes the forest by fire.

In this context, the claim that smoke produced from a forest fire extinguishes its own generator, the forest fire, is untenable; for even the forest fire extinguishes its own generator, the dry wood. Thus, because of the description of a similarity of qualities between the cause and effect—the forest fire and the smoke—it constitutes the figure of speech known as *samālaṅkāra* (Equalization).
The third type of *sama* is that where the desired end is not achieved, despite the effort of the agent toward its accomplishment.
"O brother-in-law, this acquisition of an elephant is appropriate for you, who are seeking an elephant. (91)

When the accomplishment of a task for which an agent has exerted effort occurs without the occurrence of an undesirable result, that is the third type of *sama* (the "Equal"). O brother-in-law (*syāla*), for you who seek an elephant (*vāraṇārthin*), this acquisition of an elephant (*vāraṇalābha*)—meaning the acquisition of being turned away by the king's men—is appropriate; here, because the effortless acquisition of the desired object (the elephant) is described through a superimposition of identity based on *śleṣa* (punning), it is the third *sama*. [The context is:
one who had gone to the palace gate to beg for an elephant was turned away from afar by the gatekeepers; thus, another speaks to him with derision.
O King, having sought refuge in you while crying out loudly with my elephants as if begging for wealth, I have dwelt here for a long time; this is another example of the third type of *samasa*.
You yourself grant that very same eradication to me today; for the service of the great is never in vain.

In this verse, O King, you cause me—who desire to go by mounting a lofty elephant—to attain *uccāṭana*, that is, wandering on high elephants (*uccair-gajaiḥ-aṭanam*) [or, as a euphemism, being driven far away]. Because this description portrays the attainment of the desired object without effort, it constitutes the figure of speech *samā* (similitude). Through the pun (*śleṣa*) on the word *uccāṭana*, the sense of "being driven far away" flashes forth, whereby censure is implied. 92. "Vicitra" (the Strange) occurs when an effort, directed toward a desired result, yields a contrary outcome: "The virtuous bow even before the three worlds, though they have attained supreme eminence."

If an effort contrary [to the means] is made out of a desire for a result—that is, with the longing to obtain some particular fruit—that is "the marvelous" (*vicitra*). In the case of the verse, "Those who have attained eminence bow down," bowing—which is the opposite of that [attainment]—is performed out of a desire for the fruit consisting of eminence; thus, it is marvelous. Another example of the marvelous is:
"O King, your fame purifies the worlds while seeking to stain the faces of the wicked."
Even valor causes harm to a friend when it is used to bring joy to an enemy.

Here, [the figure is] "wondrous" (*vicitra*) because it describes a contrary effort: to make something pure, one makes it impure; to bring joy to a friend (*mitra*), one acts against the friend (*mitra*, i.e., the sun).
First, there is the description of the excellence of the contained (*ādheya*) as being greater than its broad support (*adhikaraṇa*).
The cosmic eggs may find room within your waters, but your qualities cannot be contained therein. ||93||

*Adhika* (the Exceeding) is the description of the contained object as being greater than its support, which is already renowned for its extreme vastness. Because it serves as the support even for the cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*), the waters are exceedingly extensive; yet, the virtues of the two kings do not find room therein. This is *adhika* because of the description of the excellence of the virtues, which constitute the contained objects. Another example of this is: "The souls withdrawn at the time of the end of the age..."
The worlds rested within her with full expansion;
yet the joys arising from the arrival of those whose wealth is penance did not find room within the body of that enemy of Kaiṭabha.

In this context, when it is described that the fourteen worlds, which rested within the body of the Blessed One during the time of cosmic dissolution, did not find sufficient space within His body due to the joy produced by Nārada’s arrival, this is *adhika* (the "excessive") because of the description of an excess of what is contained.
The second type of *adhika* is also considered such: when the substratum is greater than the object contained within it.
Or how many gates of Brahmā are there where these qualities of yours find rest? || 94 ||

The second type of *adhika* (the "excessive") is the description of the receptacle (*ādhāra*) as being greater in extent than the contained object (*ādheya*) with which it is commonly known to be associated. (He Rāma! How small is that *vāgbrahman* (the Brahman of Speech) wherein your infinite auspicious qualities find rest and abide without crowding? What would its measure be? The meaning is that it is impossible to determine its measure by saying, "its measure is this much. Here, the superiority of the receptacle—the *śabdabrahman*—is stated in comparison to the qualities of the contained object.
Another example of this is:
"O King, oh, how vast is the interior of the three worlds!"
That mass of your glory, though immeasurable and impossible to measure, is contained herein.
The prowess displayed on the side of a powerful enemy is an adversary;
his two ears, which follow his victorious eyes, have been surpassed by his two lotuses. 95.

The *pratyanīka* ornament consists of exerting prowess against an ally (*mitra*) or other supporter belonging to the faction of a powerful and formidable enemy—precisely because one is unable to retaliate directly against that enemy.

The two ears, which follow the victorious eyes—that is, which are inclined toward following the eyes that conquer—have been "placed below" (*adhah-kṛtau*), meaning they have been surpassed or eclipsed by the two *utpala* (blue lotus) flowers. Here, because the *utpala* flowers lack the direct capacity to conquer the eyes, the ears—which are characterized by their habit of following the eyes—are "placed below. This constitutes *pratyanīka* (the counter-attack), as it describes the surpassing of the enemy's side. In the word *adhah-kṛta*, through *śleṣa* (paronomasia), there is an identification (*abhedādhyavasāya*) between "surpassing" and "being placed in a lower region."
Another example of the *pratyanīka* (counter-agent) figure is:
"O one whose heart has entered into the ocean of my beauty and fame,
Madana, as if out of malice toward you, truly torments her all the more, devoid of compassion."

In this context, the figure *pratyanīka* (counter-attack) occurs because the word "revenge" (*pratīkāra*) uttered by Madana against a handsome man who has stolen his own beauty mercilessly consumes the young woman enamored of him—thus describing the humiliation of an enemy's faction.
The figure *kāvyārthāpatti* (poetic presumption) is held to be the establishment of a meaning through the power of what is said (*kaumutyena*).
[Example: "That moon of your face has conquered [the moon]; what talk can there be of lotuses?"

The establishment of a meaning by way of *kaimutya*, that is, by the maxim of "the stick and the rice-grains" (*daṇḍāpūpika*), resulting in the accomplishment of the intended sense, is *kāvyārthāpatti* (poetic presumption). The essential definition is that where the establishment of a meaning is described according to the maxim of "the stick and the rice-grains," there is *kāvyārthāpatti*. Some maintain that the word "poetic" (*kāvya*) is included to exclude the [logical] presumption found in the scientific treatises (*śāstra*), since presumption exists there as well; however, in reality, poetic presumption is indeed distinct from the means of valid cognition known as presumption (*arthāpatti*).

He is renowned for his beauty and his power to delight; or rather, the moon—the conqueror of the lotus—has been conquered by your face. (This being so,) what talk can there be of the *sarasīruhas*, the lotuses? This is an example [of *arthāpatti*]. Here, since the moon, the conqueror of the lotus, has been conquered by him, it goes without saying that the lotuses themselves have been conquered by him; thus, because the sense of "conquering the lotuses" is established through the logic of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpika*), this is *arthāpatti*. Another example of poetic *arthāpatti* is:
"This lower lip of the tremulous-eyed one steals the luster of the *bandhujīva* flower..."
Alas, that it steals away the radiance of other living beings—what wonder is there in this?

*Bandhujīva* refers to the *bandhūka* flower; "one who steals its luster" (*tatprabhāharaḥ*) means one who steals the luster of kinsmen (*bandhūnām jīvānām*). Through a metaphorical identification (*abhedādhyavasāna*) based on paronomasia (*śleṣa*), the fact that he steals the luster of other living beings is established even though it was not explicitly stated—this is *arthāpatti* (presumption).
*Kāvyaliṅga* (poetic reason) is the justification of a point that requires justification:
"O dull-witted Kandarpa, you are conquered; the Three-eyed Lord dwells within my heart. (97)

The *alaṅkāra* named *kāvyaliṅga* is the substantiation of a matter that requires substantiation and is yet to be established. An example is: "O dull-witted, foolish Kandarpa, you have been conquered; the Three-eyed One resides in my heart. Here, because the conquest of Madana is difficult to achieve, the presentation of his conquest requires substantiation. By demonstrating the presence of the Three-eyed One, the consumer of Madana, within one's own heart, that substantiation is effected; thus, it is *kāvyaliṅga*.
A cause (hetu) may be either the meaning of a sentence (vākyārtha) or a single word (padārtha). In the example, "Trilocana is in my heart," the meaning of the sentence constitutes the cause.
Another illustration of *kāvyaliṅga* is:
"May the smearing of ashes be auspicious for you; may the rosary of Rudrākṣa beads be auspicious."
Alas! Upon this succession of steps that adorns the abode of the Beloved of the Mountain’s Daughter,
we shall today sink into the great delusion called liberation— which destroys the vision of your feet— by the Lord who has been gratified by our worship.

In this context, the fact that liberation is a great delusion is not commonly established and thus requires support; and that [support] is provided by the meaning of the phrase "which cuts off the light of the bliss of serving you. Therefore, this is *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic figure of causal indication) based on the meaning of a word (*padārthahetuka*).
The statement of two things—one general and one particular—is *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration).

The statement of a general and a particular constitutes *arthāntaranyāsa*. Of these two, one is the subject under discussion (*prastuta*) and the other is not (*aprastuta*). Consequently, when the particular is the subject under discussion, the placement of the non-subject general along with it is one type of *arthāntaranyāsa*; when the general is the subject under discussion, the placement of the particular along with it is the second type. Thus, *arthāntaranyāsa* is of two kinds. Here, this should be noted: in the placement of the general and the particular, there must necessarily be a relationship between the supported (*samarthya*) and the supporter (*samarthaka*).

In *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic figure of the indicative) as well, there exists a relationship between the supported (*samarthya*) and the supporter (*samarthaka*). This being the case, this is the distinction between *kāvyaliṅga* and *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general principle): *arthāntaranyāsa* occurs when there is a relationship of general and particular between the supported and the supporter; *kāvyaliṅga* occurs when there is a relationship such as that of producer and produced, or the like. An example of *arthāntaranyāsa*, which consists of supporting a particular by means of a general principle, is as follows: "Hanumān crossed the ocean; what is difficult for the great-souled? (98)
In this instance, the specific fact that Hanumān crossed the ocean is supported by the general principle: "What is difficult for the great-souled?
Another example of this is:
"He who protects from the sun the darkness hidden in caves, as if it were afraid of the day."
Surely even toward a lowly person who has sought refuge, those of noble mind feel a sense of "mine" as if toward a virtuous wife.
An example of *arthāntaranyāsa* in the form of supporting a general principle by means of a specific instance is as follows:
"Even a very small thing attains importance through association with a superior object;
a thread, by being attached to a garland of flowers, is worn upon the head. (99)

Even something very small or inferior attains or acquires dignity through its connection with a virtuous object. In the example, "The thread—the string—is worn on the head by virtue of its association (*anuṣaṅga*) or contact with a garland of flowers"—the general principle that an insubstantial thing attains dignity through contact with something virtuous is presented as the *prastuta* (the subject at hand); this is supported by a specific instance not under discussion (*aprastuta-viśeṣa*), namely the attainment of dignity in the form of being carried on the head due to the thread's connection with the flower garland. This constitutes the application of the definition of *arthāntaranyāsa*. Here is another example of this figure:
To those whose minds are shrouded by their own defects, even that which is exceedingly beautiful appears distorted;
one afflicted by bile perceives even a conch shell, white as the moon, as yellow.
That [king] in whom particularities and generalities were fully manifest was invincible; for the great are as unassailable as the oceans. (10)

The *vikasvara* ornament occurs in that poetry where particulars, universals, and further particulars are arranged. The essential definition is this: when, for the purpose of supporting a particular, a universal is first presented, yet the poet—unsatisfied even with its established renown—further arranges another particular either by way of simile or as an *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration), there exists the *vikasvara* ornament. For example: "That famous king was not conquered by anyone" (*na jigye*) is the presentation of the particular.

The general proposition "the great are indeed invincible" is established as a support for that [statement]. Then, by way of comparison, the specific instance "like the oceans" is presented; this specific instance reinforces the general meaning—the invincibility of the great—and thus it is the *vikasvara* ornament. Another example of *vikasvara* is: "Of Him, the source of infinite jewels, the snow did not become a destroyer of his beauty; for a single defect sinks away amidst a multitude of virtues, like the spot on the moon amidst its rays."

Here too, there is the placement of another particular instance by way of comparison; however, an example of the placement of another particular instance by way of *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration) is to be seen in the *Anubandha*.
Circuitous speech (*vakrokti*) is the construction of a secondary meaning through wordplay (*śleṣa*) or intonation (*kāku*); for example:
"Abandon your pride; the day has arrived; there is no Nandin here near Hara. (101)

*Vakrokti* (oblique speech) is the conception of another meaning—either through punning (*śleṣa*) or through intonation (*kāku*)—or the attribution of an intention to a sentence other than what was intended. For example, when a heroine is addressed by a hero who says, "O beloved, abandon your *māna* (pride/anger); the day has arrived," she replies by conceiving another meaning for the hero's words through punning: "In this place, near me, there is no *nandin* (joy), but rather [Nandin] is present near *Hara* (Śiva). Here, by means of punning, another meaning—"Do not abandon the *nandin* (the bull Nandin) that has arrived"—is conceived for the hero's statement; thus, it is *vakrokti*. Another illustration of *vakrokti*:
"Your anger is improper; you have spoken thus without due reflection.
"This is indeed not proper," she replied, and struck him with her garland.

In this instance, by means of a shift in intonation (*kāku*), the phrase "this is not at all appropriate" is interpreted as "this is indeed appropriate"; having thus constructed a different meaning, the heroine strikes the hero with a garland—this is *vakrokti* (indirect speech).
*Svabhāvokti* (description of nature) is the description of the natural state as it exists in its genus and so forth:
"With eyes wide and ears pricked, he is stared at by the deer. (102)

*Swabhāvokti* (Description of Nature) is the ornament consisting of the description of the inherent nature of an object situated in its genus and so forth, which is connected with its birth, action, quality, and so on. For example, in the verse "The deer are gazing with eyes [lit. waves] trembling, with restless glances, and with ears pricked up [lit. motionless]," there is *svabhāvokti* because of the description of the natural character of the deer (*kuraṅga*). *Bhāvika* is the description of the direct perception of past or future events. For example:
"Even now I behold the gods and demons fighting here."

*Bhāvika* is the description of a thing that has occurred or is yet to occur, as if it were being directly perceived. The essential definition is this: where the past or the future is described with the vividness of direct perception (*pratyakṣatvena*), there is the *bhāvika* ornament. For example: "I even now behold the gods and demons fighting in this very place"—here, because the past battle between the gods and the Dānavas is described as if it were being witnessed firsthand, it is the *bhāvika* ornament. The *udātta* (the exalted) is the description of prosperity, a praiseworthy deed, or other such [magnificent] characteristics. For instance: "On the mountain peak of that Lord whose crown is the matted locks of Śiva, the battle took place. (104)

*Ṛddhi* means prosperity, success, or abundance; *anyopalakṣaṇa* refers to praiseworthy conduct and noble character. Where prosperity and success are described, there is the figure of speech *udātta*. The meaning is that where praiseworthy conduct, which is subordinate to something else (*anya-aṅga*), is described, there too the figure of speech is *udātta*. By the word *upalakṣaṇa*, subordination (*aṅgatva*) itself is intended here.

On the peak of that Himālaya where the famous battle between Śiva and Arjuna—the two who wear the crown of Dhūrjaṭi—took place, that very Himavat is meant [by the pronoun "this"]. Here, the praiseworthy deed of the battle between Śiva and Arjuna is described as a subordinate element to the greatness of the Himavat; thus, this is the figure of speech *udātta* (the Sublime). An example of *udātta* consisting of the description of prosperity (*ṛddhi*) is as follows:
"Reflected in the jeweled walls and surrounded by hundreds of reflections, the Lord of Laṅkā was recognized in his true form only with great difficulty by the son of Añjanā."
Here, the figure of speech is *udātta* (the sublime), as the abundance of Rāvaṇa’s prosperity is described.
